most_important_collaboration: Lakshya (2004), the only one of the two in which Bachchan plays a character.
biography: Ritesh Sidhwani and Farhan Akhtar founded Excel Entertainment in 1999 and made Dil Chahta Hai two years later, a film widely treated as the point at which mainstream Hindi cinema started speaking in a recognisably contemporary urban register; it won the National Award for Best Feature Film in Hindi, as Rock On!! later did. Excel went on to Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara, Dil Dhadakne Do, the Fukrey films and Gully Boy, and was among the first Indian houses to build a serious streaming slate, with Inside Edge nominated at the International Emmys and Mirzapur and Made in Heaven following. His two Bachchan credits are Lakshya, where Bachchan plays the commanding officer, and 120 Bahadur, where he narrates. His article does not mention Bachchan. Read alongside PERSON-152: the two men are business partners and this workbook counts the same two films for each. The entry is graded High.

name: Rohan Vinayak
career_background: Not an individual: the credit is a music director duo billed professionally as Rohan–Vinayak, described as such in trade coverage. The roster name is a parsing artifact created when the duo's hyphenated billing was flattened into a single personal name. No birth dates or individual biographical detail could be established for either member.
debut: Not established; Nil Battey Sannata is among their earliest reported credits.
major_works: Nil Battey Sannata; Sarkar 3 (2017); 102 Not Out (2018); Lootcase; Tarla; the series Break Point and Subedaar
recurring_themes: Songs for mid-budget films and series, generally sharing a soundtrack with other composers.
historical_importance: Not established. The pair are recorded because they carry a song-composing credit on two films in this filmography.
relationship_with_actor: Two films in consecutive years, both Bachchan leads. On Sarkar 3 (2017) the music is credited to the duo with Ravi Shankar; Bachchan returns as Subhash Nagre in the third and last of the series. On 102 Not Out (2018) the songs are credited to Salim–Sulaiman, Amitabh Bachchan himself and the duo, with George Joseph writing the background score; the duo also produced the track 'Badumbaaa', which Bachchan composed and which he sings with Rishi Kapoor. That production credit is the closest documented working contact between them and the actor, and it puts them in the unusual position of producing a Bachchan composition.
most_important_collaboration: 102 Not Out (2018), where they worked directly on a song composed and sung by Bachchan.
biography: This row records a duo under a name that does not belong to a person. Bollywood Hungama and Filmibeat both describe Rohan–Vinayak as a music director duo, and the 102 Not Out wikitext preserves the hyphen — 'Rohan-Vinayak' — while the Sarkar 3 wikitext writes 'Rohan Vinayak' without it, which is where the artifact originates. This is the third such case in this workbook, after 'BapiTutul', whose en-dash template was stripped, and 'Kedar Bhargav', which is the duo Kedar Upadhyay and Bhargav Purohit. Their two credits here are both Bachchan leads: Sarkar 3, the last of Ram Gopal Varma's trilogy, and 102 Not Out, in which Bachchan plays a 102-year-old man and also takes a composing credit of his own — the duo produced that song. The roster was frozen before the artifact was found, so the row stands under the wrong name and records the correction. The entry is graded Low.

name: Romesh Sharma
career_background: Romesh Brij Sharma, born 27 July 1947, an Indian producer, actor and director who has worked in film and television for over thirty years under his banner Romesh Films. He became known as an actor in Conrad Rooks's 1972 American film Siddhartha, and in the 1980s his company Sharma Limited founded Cloud 9 Studio at Baie du Tombeau in Mauritius, used by film-makers from India, South Africa, Japan and Mauritius; in 2014 the company announced plans to demolish it for a hotel.
debut: Acting from 1972; producing from the 1980s, with Diljalaa (1987) among his earlier credits.
major_works: Siddhartha (1972, as actor); The Burning Train (1980, as actor); Diljalaa (1987); Hum (1991); Suhaag (1994); Dil Jo Bhi Kahey... (2005)
recurring_themes: Large-cast commercial entertainment as producer, and, as director, a late turn to material drawn from Mauritius, where his studio was.
creative_style: Primarily a producer and facilitator who also acted and, once, directed; his own film adapts a Mauritian television series he had a hand in.
historical_importance: Not a shaping figure, but Hum is a significant commercial film and Cloud 9 gave Hindi cinema a working base in Mauritius for two decades.
relationship_with_actor: Two films fourteen years apart, in different capacities. He produced Hum (1991), in which Bachchan plays Tiger and then Shekhar Malhotra, one of the last major hits before his withdrawal from the screen and the source of the song 'Jumma Chumma De De'; Sharma also took a small acting role in it as the brother of Kimi Katkar's character. He then directed, produced and wrote Dil Jo Bhi Kahey... (2005), shot in Mauritius, adapted from the Mauritian television series C'est La Vie and featuring his own son Karan Sharma, with Bachchan in support. The first is a major film, the second a personal one.
most_important_collaboration: Hum (1991), a large commercial success and one of the last hits of Bachchan's first career.
biography: Romesh Sharma has been a producer, actor and occasional director since the early 1970s, when he appeared in Conrad Rooks's Siddhartha. His most notable production is Hum (1991), the Mukul S. Anand film in which Bachchan plays a dockworker turned respectable man, a hit that came just before the collapse of his box-office position; Sharma also appears in it briefly. In the 1980s his company built Cloud 9 Studio in Mauritius, where parts of Kuch Kuch Hota Hai, Armaan and Hello Brother were shot, and in 2005 he used it for his own film as director, Dil Jo Bhi Kahey..., adapted from a Mauritian television series and casting his son alongside Bachchan. A credit conflict is recorded rather than smoothed: the Silsila article states that Romesh Sharma wrote that film's dialogue, but Silsila's writing credits in this workbook's Films sheet do not include him, so the frozen roster counts two films rather than three. The entry is graded High.

name: Rupam Chitra
career_background: A production banner associated with the Hrishikesh Mukherjee and N. C. Sippy partnership and, later, with the younger Sippys. No founding date or ownership record could be established; it is documented through the films that carry its name.
debut: Chupke Chupke (1975) is the earliest credit located for the banner.
major_works: Chupke Chupke (1975); Satte Pe Satta (1982)
recurring_themes: Comedy of deception — an elaborate practical joke sustained across a household in the first film, seven brothers passing themselves off in the second.
historical_importance: Not independently established, but it carries the credit on Chupke Chupke, one of the most enduring Hindi comedies.
relationship_with_actor: Two films seven years apart, both comedies and both with Bachchan in a different register from his usual one. Chupke Chupke (1975), directed by Hrishikesh Mukherjee and produced by Mukherjee with N. C. Sippy, casts him as Sukumar Sinha in support of Dharmendra's central imposture — a rare light supporting turn made at the height of the angry-young-man cycle. Satte Pe Satta (1982), directed by Raj N. Sippy and produced by Romu N. Sippy, casts him as Ravi Anand in a double role, leading the seven brothers of a Seven Brides for Seven Brothers adaptation. The banner is the thread between the older Sippy generation and the younger.
most_important_collaboration: Chupke Chupke (1975), the more durable film, though Satte Pe Satta gives Bachchan much the larger part.
biography: Rupam Chitra appears in the studio field of two films seven years apart, and the interest of the row is who stands behind them. Chupke Chupke was produced by Hrishikesh Mukherjee with N. C. Sippy, the partnership that also made Abhimaan and Mili in this filmography; Satte Pe Satta was directed by Raj N. Sippy and produced by Romu N. Sippy, N. C. Sippy's son. The banner therefore tracks a family and a working relationship across a generational handover, from Mukherjee's understated comedies to a broad 1982 star vehicle. N. C. Sippy, Romu N. Sippy and Hrishikesh Mukherjee are all already entries in this roster, as is Mohini N. Sippy, a writer on two of the same group's films and a separate entry in this batch. No Wikipedia article for the banner exists and no founding date or ownership detail was located, so the row rests on the two films and a search summary. The entry is graded Low.

name: S. D. Burman
career_background: Sachin Dev Burman (1 October 1906 – 31 October 1975), a member of the Tripura royal family, born in Comilla in present-day Bangladesh. He began with Bengali films in 1937 and became one of the most successful and influential composers in Hindi cinema, scoring over 100 films across four decades. He also sang, recording 14 Hindi and 13 Bengali film songs in a folk and light semi-classical style drawn from East Bengal.
debut: Bengali films from 1937; a long Hindi career followed from the 1940s.
major_works: Over 100 soundtracks, among them Pyaasa, Kaagaz Ke Phool, Guide, Aradhana, Abhimaan (1973), Chupke Chupke (1975) and Mili (1975)
recurring_themes: Folk melody from East Bengal absorbed into film song, and an unusual willingness to let a voice carry a scene unadorned.
creative_style: A melodist whose settings are spare by the standards of his era, and who worked repeatedly with the leading playback singers of four decades.
major_awards: Sangeet Natak Akademi Award (1958); Padma Shri (1969); National Film Award for Best Male Playback Singer for Aradhana (1970); National Film Award for Best Music Direction for Zindagi Zindagi (1974); a commemorative postage stamp in 2007.
historical_importance: One of the two or three most important composers in the history of Hindi film music, and the father of R. D. Burman, who succeeded him and who is the single most frequent collaborator in this entire filmography.
relationship_with_actor: This row and PERSON-207 are the same man, split across two entries by a naming error in the frozen roster, and between them they account for four films. Under this entry he scores Chupke Chupke (1975), in which Bachchan plays Sukumar Sinha, released in the last year of Burman's life — he died that October. The second credit is posthumous by forty-seven years: Chup: Revenge of the Artist (2022) uses his songs, recreated by Sneha Khanwalkar, in a film whose subject is Guru Dutt, for whom Burman had scored Pyaasa and Kaagaz Ke Phool. Bachchan appears in Chup as himself. The pairing of a 1975 score and a 2022 recreation inside one row is an accident of the roster that turns out to describe something real about his afterlife.
most_important_collaboration: Chupke Chupke (1975), a living score for a Bachchan film, as against the posthumous recreation in Chup.
biography: S. D. Burman is among the handful of composers who defined Hindi film music, working from the 1940s to his death in 1975 across Pyaasa, Kaagaz Ke Phool, Guide and Aradhana, and drawing throughout on the folk music of East Bengal, which he also sang. He was born into the Tripura royal family, won the Padma Shri in 1969 and National Awards as both singer and composer, and was commemorated on a postage stamp in 2007. This workbook carries him twice, because the frozen roster records 'S. D. Burman' and 'Sachin Dev Burman' as two people: a fetch of the second name redirects to the first and returns a byte-identical article, which is how the duplication was caught. The two rows together cover Chupke Chupke and Chup here, and Abhimaan and Mili under PERSON-207. One further connection dominates: his son R. D. Burman is PERSON-001 in this roster with thirty films, more than any other collaborator, so father and son between them span almost the whole of Bachchan's career in music. The entry is graded High.

name: Sachin Dev Burman
career_background: The same person as PERSON-206: Sachin Dev Burman (1 October 1906 – 31 October 1975), member of the Tripura royal family, born in Comilla, active from 1932, composer of over 100 film soundtracks and father of R. D. Burman. This entry exists because the frozen roster recorded his full name and his initials as two separate collaborators.
debut: Bengali films from 1937; Hindi films from the 1940s.
major_works: Pyaasa; Kaagaz Ke Phool; Guide; Aradhana; Abhimaan (1973); Mili (1975); Chupke Chupke (1975)
recurring_themes: East Bengali folk melody carried into film song; songs written to sit inside a scene rather than interrupt it.
creative_style: Spare, melody-first scoring, and a composer who used silence and a single voice more readily than most of his contemporaries.
major_awards: Sangeet Natak Akademi Award (1958); Padma Shri (1969); National Film Award for Best Male Playback Singer for Aradhana (1970); National Film Award for Best Music Direction for Zindagi Zindagi (1974).
historical_importance: See PERSON-206: one of the most important composers in Indian cinema, and the father of this filmography's most frequent collaborator.
relationship_with_actor: Under this duplicate entry fall the two Hrishikesh Mukherjee films whose music is central to Bachchan's early career. Abhimaan (1973) is the more important by far: Burman's score is the substance of a film about two singers whose marriage collapses when the wife's career outgrows the husband's, with Bachchan as Subir Kumar opposite Jaya Bhaduri, and the songs are doing the narrative work that dialogue usually does. Mili (1975) followed, with Bachchan as the withdrawn alcoholic Shekhar and a score written in the last year of Burman's life. His other two Bachchan credits sit under PERSON-206.
most_important_collaboration: Abhimaan (1973), where the score carries the film and the marriage at its centre.
biography: This entry is a duplicate of PERSON-206 and describes the same composer; both are retained because the roster was frozen before the duplication was found, and neither can be deleted without shifting every subsequent person id. The split is not arbitrary in its effects: the two rows happen to divide his four Bachchan films into the two Hrishikesh Mukherjee pictures recorded here — Abhimaan and Mili, both produced by N. C. Sippy and both written in part by Mohini N. Sippy, a separate entry in this batch — and the Chupke Chupke and Chup credits recorded there. Abhimaan is the significant one for this project's purposes, since its songs are the mechanism by which the marriage at its centre is built and then broken, and it remains among the most discussed romantic films in Bachchan's filmography. Burman died on 31 October 1975, weeks after Mili's release. The duplication is recorded here and in the source row rather than silently corrected. The entry is graded High.

name: Sagar Sarhadi
industry: Hindi cinema; Urdu literature and theatre
career_background: Born Ganga Sagar Talwar on 11 May 1933 in Baffa, Mansehra district, in present-day Pakistan, son of Than Singh Talwar and Prem Dai and uncle of the director Ramesh Talwar. He wrote Urdu short stories and plays before entering film, and continued as a writer, director and producer. He died in Mumbai on 22 March 2021.
debut: Dialogue on Goonj and Alingan (1974); his breakthrough was Kabhi Kabhie (1976).
major_works: Kabhi Kabhie (1976); Noorie (1979); Silsila (1981); Bazaar (1982, as director); Chandni (1989); Faasle; Rang (1993)
recurring_themes: Romantic longing and its social cost — love deferred by marriage, love conducted outside it, and in Bazaar the sale of a young woman into marriage.
creative_style: An Urdu writer's sensibility applied to mainstream romance: restraint, literary dialogue, and a willingness to leave a relationship unresolved rather than punish it.
major_awards: A Lifetime Achievement Award at the International Cultural Artifact Film Festival.
historical_importance: One of the principal writers of the Yash Chopra romance, and as a director the maker of Bazaar, a serious film about bride-buying in Hyderabad.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, and for a project centred on Bachchan's romantic persona they are among the most important in the entire roster. He wrote the screenplay and dialogue of Kabhi Kabhie (1976), in which Bachchan plays Amit, the poet who gives up the woman he loves to her arranged marriage and meets her again two decades later — the film that showed he could carry a romantic lead rather than an action one. He then wrote the screenplay of Silsila (1981), co-writing the story with Preeti Bedi while Yash Chopra co-wrote the screenplay and Romesh Sharma supplied the dialogue; Bachchan plays Amit Malhotra in the film that the Silsila article calls the first Hindi film about an extramarital relationship, opposite Jaya Bachchan and Rekha. No other two-film writer in this roster is so directly responsible for the shape of his romantic image.
most_important_collaboration: Kabhi Kabhie (1976), which established Bachchan as a romantic lead and remains the defining film of that side of his persona.
biography: Sagar Sarhadi came to Hindi cinema from Urdu literature, having written short stories and plays, and was born in what is now Pakistan as Ganga Sagar Talwar. Yash Chopra's Kabhi Kabhie made him in 1976, and the two films he wrote for that banner — Kabhi Kabhie and Silsila — are the pair that define Bachchan as a romantic actor rather than an angry one. Kabhi Kabhie gave him Amit the poet, renouncing love and living with the consequence for twenty years; Silsila gave him an adulterous affair played opposite his own wife and Rekha, a piece of casting that the film has never been discussed apart from. Sarhadi also wrote Noorie and Chandni for the same house, and directed Bazaar in 1982, a hard film about the sale of young women into marriage that is his own favourite among his work. He died in Mumbai in 2021. The digest parser copied his birth date into the death field; both dates here come from the lead prose. The entry is graded High.

name: Sahara One Motion Pictures
career_background: Also known as Sahara Movie Studios and Sahara Motion Pictures, the film arm of the Sahara India Pariwar conglomerate, with Subrata Roy as chief executive and Sandeep Bhargava as chief operating officer. It produced and distributed films from 2004 to 2014.
debut: Its first slate came in 2004 and included Sheen, Kyun! Ho Gaya Na..., Run, Gayab, Naach, Inteqam and Phir Milenge.
major_works: Kyun! Ho Gaya Na... (2004); Phir Milenge (2004); Naach (2004); No Entry (2005); Home Delivery (2005); Darna Zaroori Hai (2006)
recurring_themes: A broad, unfocused commercial slate typical of a conglomerate entering film — comedy, remakes of southern hits, issue films and Ram Gopal Varma productions side by side.
historical_importance: A decade-long attempt by a large Indian conglomerate to operate as a film studio, ending in 2014; notable as a corporate episode more than a creative one.
relationship_with_actor: Two films two years apart, both minor for Bachchan. Kyun! Ho Gaya Na... (2004), co-produced with Boney Kapoor and BSK Network, casts him as Raj Chauhan in support. Darna Zaroori Hai (2006), co-produced with Ram Gopal Varma's RGV Film Company, casts him as Professor Sunil Khanna in one segment of a horror anthology. Neither film was built around him, and the banner's article does not mention him.
most_important_collaboration: Kyun! Ho Gaya Na... (2004), marginally the more substantial of two small roles.
biography: Sahara Movie Studios was the film division of Sahara India Pariwar, the conglomerate run by Subrata Roy, and it produced and distributed for a decade from 2004 before ceasing in 2014. Its slate was wide and undisciplined — in 2004 alone it backed Govind Nihalani-adjacent issue films, a Tamil remake, a Ram Gopal Varma production and a Kashmir drama — and it is remembered less for any film than as an instance of conglomerate money entering Hindi cinema and leaving again. Its two Bachchan credits are both supporting or segment roles: Kyun! Ho Gaya Na..., which it co-produced with Boney Kapoor, a separate entry in this roster, and Darna Zaroori Hai, co-produced with RGV Film Company, a separate entry in this batch. The article was fetched under the resolved title 'Sahara Movie Studios' and names Kyun! Ho Gaya Na... in its filmography with Kapoor's co-producing credit. The entry is graded Medium.

name: Sajid-Farhad
career_background: A writing and directing duo of brothers, Sajid Samji and Farhad Samji, born into an Aga Khani (Khoja) Nizari Ismaili family. They began as lyricists, brought in by David Dhawan for Hum Kisise Kum Nahin (2002), and had their first success with 'M Bole Toh' from Munna Bhai M.B.B.S. Ram Gopal Varma then hired them as writers, after which they became Rohit Shetty's regular dialogue writers.
debut: As lyricists, Hum Kisise Kum Nahin (2002); as writers, Shiva (2006) for Ram Gopal Varma; as directors, Entertainment (2014).
major_works: Golmaal Returns (2008); All the Best (2009); Golmaal 3 and Singham (2010); Ready (2011); Housefull 2 and Bol Bachchan (2012); Chennai Express and Himmatwala (2013); Entertainment (2014); Housefull 3 (2016)
recurring_themes: Broad comedy built on wordplay, mistaken meaning and punning dialogue — the register of the Golmaal and Housefull franchises.
creative_style: Dialogue and lyric specialists rather than structural writers, brought in to supply the jokes; five of the films they wrote have passed 100 crore.
historical_importance: Among the most commercially successful comedy writers of the 2010s, central to the Rohit Shetty comedy cycle.
relationship_with_actor: Two films five years apart, and both connect to the duo's two employers. They wrote Ram Gopal Varma Ki Aag (2007), the Sholay remake in which Bachchan plays Babban Singh, the Gabbar figure — a notorious failure and the least well-regarded film of his late career — and also wrote lyrics for it. They then wrote the dialogue and lyrics of Bol Bachchan (2012) for Rohit Shetty, a comedy whose title plays on the actor's name and in which Bachchan appears as himself in the opening. The pairing moves from his worst role to a film that uses his surname as a pun.
most_important_collaboration: Bol Bachchan (2012), a large commercial success, though Aag gives Bachchan much the bigger part.
biography: Sajid and Farhad Samji began as lyricists and became the most reliable comedy dialogue writers in Hindi cinema, working first for Ram Gopal Varma and then for Rohit Shetty on the Golmaal and Singham films, with five of their scripts passing the 100-crore mark; they started directing with Entertainment in 2014. Their two credits in this filmography are unusually far apart in quality. Ram Gopal Varma Ki Aag, in 2007, recast Sholay with Bachchan as the villain and is widely treated as one of the worst Hindi films of its decade. Bol Bachchan, in 2012, is a Rohit Shetty comedy whose punning title turns on Bachchan's own name, and in which he appears as himself. The duo's name is correctly hyphenated in the roster, unlike three other composing duos in this workbook, which were flattened into single fictitious names. The entry is graded High.

name: Sajid–Wajid
career_background: A Hindi film music director duo of brothers, Sajid Khan and Wajid Khan, sons of the tabla player Sharafat Ali Khan. They worked together from 1998 until Wajid Khan's death on 1 June 2020, after which Sajid Khan has continued alone. They were closely associated with Salman Khan's films.
debut: Composing from 1998; their commercial peak came with Dabangg (2010).
major_works: Hello Brother (1999); Tere Naam (2003); Partner (2007); God Tussi Great Ho (2008); Dabangg (2010); Ek Tha Tiger (2012); Dabangg 3 (2019)
recurring_themes: High-energy mass entertainers, particularly for Salman Khan, mixing qawwali and Sufi textures with dance production.
creative_style: A duo writing for the star rather than the film, with a strong sense of what will work as a single.
major_awards: Their awards list records the 2011 Filmfare Award for Best Music Direction, Zee Cine, Guild and GiMA awards, and two 2010 Mirchi Music Awards, all for Dabangg.
historical_importance: Among the defining composers of the Salman Khan vehicle, and of the 2000s and 2010s mass-entertainer soundtrack.
relationship_with_actor: Two films nine years apart, in both of which Bachchan is barely present. They scored Hello Brother (1999), a Salman Khan comedy in which Bachchan is heard only as the voice of God, sharing the music credit with Himesh Reshammiya. They then scored God Tussi Great Ho (2008), in which Bachchan plays God on screen this time, in a supporting role, with Salim–Sulaiman writing the background score. The coincidence that both of their Bachchan films cast him as God, once as a voice and once in person, is the only pattern the pairing offers.
most_important_collaboration: God Tussi Great Ho (2008), the only one of the two in which Bachchan appears on screen.
biography: Sajid and Wajid Khan, sons of the tabla player Sharafat Ali Khan, composed together for twenty-two years and were most closely identified with Salman Khan's films, from Tere Naam through Partner to Dabangg, whose soundtrack brought them the Filmfare Award for Best Music Direction in 2011 along with Zee Cine, Guild, GiMA and Mirchi awards. Wajid Khan died on 1 June 2020 and Sajid has worked alone since. Their two credits in this filmography are both Salman Khan comedies at the margins of Bachchan's career, and both, by coincidence, cast him as God: as an unseen voice in Hello Brother in 1999, and as a character in God Tussi Great Ho in 2008. Their article does not mention Bachchan. Unlike several other duos in this roster, their name survived phase-1 extraction with its en dash intact. The entry is graded High.

name: Salim Khan
career_background: Born 24 November 1935 in Indore, an Indian screenwriter, actor and producer, best known as one half of Salim–Javed with Javed Akhtar. He acted from 1960 to 1969 before turning to writing, worked with Akhtar from 1971 to 1982, and continued alone afterwards. Within the partnership he principally developed stories and characters while Akhtar handled dialogue and screenplay.
debut: Acting from 1960; screenwriting from about 1969, with the Salim–Javed partnership running from 1971.
major_works: As Salim–Javed: Seeta Aur Geeta (1972); Zanjeer (1973); Yaadon Ki Baaraat (1973); Majboor (1974); Deewaar (1975); Sholay (1975); Immaan Dharam (1977); Trishul (1978); Don (1978); Shakti (1982). Solo: Toofan (1989); Akayla (1991)
recurring_themes: The wronged son, the mother as moral centre, the state as either absent or corrupt, and the man who takes justice into his own hands — the architecture of the angry-young-man film.
creative_style: A story and structure writer: he built the premises and the characters, and the partnership's habit of writing for a specific actor is what made those characters fit Bachchan so exactly.
major_awards: His article's Filmfare table lists nominations for Zanjeer (Best Screenplay, Best Story, 1974), Deewaar (Best Dialogue, Screenplay, Story, 1976) and Shakti (Best Screenplay, 1983), but leaves every Outcome cell blank.
historical_importance: With Javed Akhtar, among the most influential screenwriters in Indian film history: the pair were the first Indian screenwriters to achieve star billing, transformed the commercial narrative formula, and created the angry-young-man archetype that defined Bachchan's career.
relationship_with_actor: No collaborator in this roster has a larger claim on Bachchan's career and a smaller film count, and the reason is bookkeeping. This workbook counts Salim–Javed as a separate team entry, so only Salim Khan's two solo credits fall under this person id: Toofan (1989), which he wrote with K. K. Shukla, and Akayla (1991), both late films for Ramesh Sippy and Ketan Desai respectively. His real significance lies in the team's work, which his own article states plainly: Salim–Javed created the angry-young-man archetype that defined Bachchan's career, Salim Khan was instrumental in launching him when he was a struggling actor, the pair insisted on casting him in lead roles, and Khan personally introduced him to Prakash Mehra and Manmohan Desai — the two directors who between them made much of his stardom.
most_important_collaboration: Under this entry, Toofan (1989); in substance, the Salim–Javed films counted elsewhere, above all Zanjeer and Deewaar.
biography: Salim Khan acted through the 1960s without much success and then, with Javed Akhtar, rewrote the terms of Hindi commercial cinema. Between 1971 and 1982 Salim–Javed wrote Zanjeer, Deewaar, Sholay, Trishul, Don and Shakti, were the first Indian screenwriters to be billed like stars, and built the figure of the angry young man around a specific actor. Khan's article states that he was instrumental in launching Bachchan, that the pair insisted on casting him when producers would not, and that Khan introduced him to Prakash Mehra and Manmohan Desai. The two films counted here are not those: they are his solo scripts from after the partnership ended, Toofan and Akayla, both made as Bachchan's stardom was fading. The low count is an artefact of the roster treating Salim–Javed as its own entry, and the row should be read with that entry rather than against it. His article's Filmfare table leaves every outcome blank, so no win is asserted from it. The entry is graded High.

name: Sanchit Balhara
career_background: One half of the film score composing duo Sanchit Balhara and Ankit Balhara, brothers born in Sonipat, Haryana, to the Haryanvi singer, actor and filmmaker Bhal Singh Balhara and the national-level athlete Mukta Chaudhary. Sanchit studied classical music in London and began as a solo composer; his elder brother Ankit joined him in 2018, and they have composed together since Manikarnika. Ankit is married to the field hockey player Savita Punia.
debut: Tera Mera Vaada (2012, Haryanvi) as a solo composer; his breakthrough was the score of Bajirao Mastani (2015).
major_works: Bajirao Mastani (2015); Padmaavat (2018); Manikarnika: The Queen of Jhansi, Kalank and War (2019); Panga (2020); Gangubai Kathiawadi and Radhe Shyam (2022)
recurring_themes: Large-scale orchestral underscore for period and historical spectacle, particularly for Sanjay Leela Bhansali.
creative_style: Symphonic scoring at scale — choirs, strings and percussion written to match very large production design rather than to sit under dialogue.
major_awards: The article's prose credits IIFA, Mirchi Music, GIMA and Zee Cine awards for the Bajirao Mastani score; its own awards table leaves every Result cell blank, so these are recorded as prose claims.
historical_importance: The house score composers of the Bhansali period epic, and among the most prominent Indian film score specialists of the last decade.
relationship_with_actor: Two films three years apart, and in both Bachchan is the narrator rather than a character. Manikarnika: The Queen of Jhansi (2019) is the first film the brothers scored together, and Bachchan opens it in voice-over; Radhe Shyam (2022) is a bilingual for which they wrote the Hindi-version score while S. Thaman scored the Telugu, and Bachchan again narrates the Hindi version. The pairing is a technical one with no evidence of direct contact, and it is characteristic of how late-period producers use his voice to frame a film aimed at a wide audience.
most_important_collaboration: Manikarnika: The Queen of Jhansi (2019), the larger film and the brothers' first as a duo.
biography: Sanchit Balhara is recorded in the frozen roster under his own name, but the Wikipedia article resolves to 'Sanchit Balhara and Ankit Balhara', a duo: Sanchit worked alone until 2018, and his elder brother joined from Manikarnika onward, which means one of the two films counted here is solo work in name only. They come from a Haryanvi film family in Sonipat, Sanchit trained in classical music in London, and his reputation was made by the score of Bajirao Mastani for Sanjay Leela Bhansali, after which they became the house composers of the Bhansali period epic, from Padmaavat to Gangubai Kathiawadi. Both of their credits in this filmography are films where Bachchan only narrates. Their awards table, like several others in this batch, leaves every result cell blank while the prose claims wins, so no win is asserted here. The entry is graded Medium.

name: Sandeep Chowta
career_background: Born in 1967 or 1968 in Buduburam, Ghana, he is an Indian music director working primarily in Hindi and Telugu cinema, active from 1996, and head of Columbia Records in India. He has composed for twelve Telugu films, sings some of his own songs, produced the anti-substance-abuse documentary Dead End in 2003, and has been a core member of the world and new age group AO Music since 2004.
debut: Composing from 1996; his best-known early work came through Ram Gopal Varma's productions.
major_works: Satya (1998); Kaun (1999); Jungle (2000); Company (2002); Boom (2003); Om Shanti Om (2007, background score); AO Music albums
recurring_themes: Hard-edged urban crime scoring, particularly for Ram Gopal Varma, set against a separate career in ambient and world music.
creative_style: A composer equally at home writing songs and underscore, whose film work is marked by electronic textures and a preference for atmosphere over melody.
historical_importance: Central to the sound of the Ram Gopal Varma crime film of the late 1990s and early 2000s, a cycle that reset the register of Hindi urban thrillers.
relationship_with_actor: Two films four years apart, in different functions and both marginal for the composer's relationship with the actor. He wrote the songs of Boom (2003), sharing the credit with Tavlin Singh, in which Bachchan plays a criminal — a film widely dismissed on release. He then wrote the background score of Om Shanti Om (2007), in which Bachchan appears as himself, with Vishal–Shekhar writing the songs. The split between song credit on one and score credit on the other is why this row carries both functions.
most_important_collaboration: Om Shanti Om (2007), by far the more successful film, though his contribution to it is underscore.
biography: Sandeep Chowta was born in Ghana and became one of the defining composers of the Ram Gopal Varma crime cycle, writing for Satya, Kaun, Jungle and Company at the point when those films were changing what a Hindi thriller sounded like. He also heads Columbia Records in India and has had a parallel career in world and ambient music as a core member of AO Music, whose albums have charted internationally since 2009. His two credits here are slighter: the songs of Boom, a 2003 film in which Bachchan plays a criminal and which was poorly received, and the background score of Om Shanti Om, Farah Khan's hit in which Bachchan appears as himself, written alongside Vishal–Shekhar's songs. His article gives his birth year only as 1967 or 1968, so the birth-year column is left blank, and it does not mention Bachchan or either film. The entry is graded Medium.

name: Sandesh Shandilya
career_background: Born 19 February 1968 in Agra, an Indian film composer, musician and singer who took his basic training from the sarangi player Ustad Sultan Khan. He has composed for over twenty film soundtracks since 2001 and has also released non-film albums.
debut: Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham (2001), on which he composed four songs alongside Jatin–Lalit and Aadesh Shrivastava.
major_works: Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham (2001); Agni Varsha (2002); Chameli (2004); Socha Na Tha (2005); Jab We Met (2007); the album Piya Basanti (2001)
recurring_themes: Melodic, semi-classical songwriting with a strong debt to his sarangi training, generally in the romantic register.
creative_style: A melodist who works well as one of several composers on a large soundtrack, supplying the slower and more classical numbers.
major_awards: Nominated, jointly with Jatin–Lalit and Aadesh Shrivastava, for the Filmfare Award for Best Music Director for Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham; his album Piya Basanti won the International Viewers' Choice Award at the 2001 MTV Video Music Awards.
historical_importance: His four songs for Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham, including 'Suraj Hua Maddham' and 'You Are My Soniya', are among the most widely heard Hindi film songs of the 2000s.
relationship_with_actor: Two films in consecutive years, both from the start of his career. He made his debut on Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham (2001), composing 'Suraj Hua Maddham', 'You Are My Soniya', 'Deewana Hai Dekho' and 'Vande Mataram' for a soundtrack that sold 2.5 million units in thirty days and 3.5 million across the year; Bachchan plays Yashvardhan Raichand, the patriarch, as an ensemble lead. He then scored Agni Varsha (2002), in which Bachchan makes an extended special appearance as Indra. The first is among the biggest soundtracks of the decade, the second a small film that failed.
most_important_collaboration: Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham (2001), his debut and a soundtrack that sold millions.
biography: Sandesh Shandilya trained under the sarangi master Ustad Sultan Khan and entered Hindi cinema at the top, sharing Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham's soundtrack with Jatin–Lalit and Aadesh Shrivastava and writing four of its songs, among them 'Suraj Hua Maddham' and 'You Are My Soniya'. The album was the best-selling of its year in India and brought the three composers a joint Filmfare nomination. In the same period his non-film album Piya Basanti, sung by Sultan Khan and K. S. Chithra, won an International Viewers' Choice Award at the MTV VMAs. He went on to Chameli, Socha Na Tha and a guest composition for Jab We Met. His second credit in this filmography, Agni Varsha (2002), is an adaptation of a Girish Karnad play in which Bachchan appears briefly as Indra. His article does not mention Bachchan. The entry is graded High.

name: Sanjay Dayma
career_background: An Indian screenwriter, dialogue writer and director, known for his work on Ashutosh Gowariker's Lagaan and for directing Ramji Londonwaley. No birth date or fuller biography could be established.
debut: Not established; Lagaan (2001) is the earliest of his credits located here.
major_works: Lagaan: Once Upon a Time in India (2001); Ramji Londonwaley (2005)
recurring_themes: Too small a documented body of work to establish one; the two films are a period sports epic and a fish-out-of-water comedy.
historical_importance: Not independently established, but he shares the screenplay credit on Lagaan, among the most acclaimed Hindi films of its era.
relationship_with_actor: Two films four years apart, in neither of which Bachchan plays a character. He shares the screenplay credit on Lagaan (2001) with Ashutosh Gowariker and Kumar Dave; Bachchan is the film's narrator, the same function Gowariker gave him again on Jodhaa Akbar. He then directed and co-wrote Ramji Londonwaley (2005), in which Bachchan appears as himself. The pairing is one narration and one self appearance, with no documented contact between writer and actor.
most_important_collaboration: Lagaan (2001), much the more significant film, though Bachchan's role in it is narration.
biography: Sanjay Dayma is credited on the screenplay of Lagaan alongside its director Ashutosh Gowariker and Kumar Dave, and directed and co-wrote Ramji Londonwaley in 2005, working on the screenplay and dialogue for that film's London sections. He has no Wikipedia article and no birth date or career detail was located. Two corrections are recorded rather than repeated. An IMDb biography states that he was nominated at the Academy Awards for Best Screenplay for Lagaan in 2002; that is wrong, and Lagaan's own article is explicit that its nomination was for Best Foreign Language Film, the third and, as of 2025, last Indian film to be nominated in that category. Separately, the Lagaan wikitext spells his name 'Sanjay Damya', while this workbook and other sources use 'Sanjay Dayma'. Gowariker, who used Bachchan as narrator on both of his own films in this filmography, is already in this roster. The entry is graded Low.

name: Sanjay Gupta
career_background: Born 14 April 1967 in Mumbai, an Indian filmmaker, producer and screenwriter working in Hindi films since 1994, known largely for remaking American action-thriller and crime films and for casting Sanjay Dutt and John Abraham repeatedly.
debut: Aatish (1994).
major_works: Aatish (1994); Kaante (2002); Musafir (2004); Zinda (2006); Shootout at Lokhandwala (2007, as producer and writer); Shootout at Wadala (2013); Jazbaa (2015); Kaabil (2017); Mumbai Saga (2021)
recurring_themes: Urban crime and male-ensemble heist or revenge plots, frequently adapted from a specific foreign film, shot in a heavily stylised register.
creative_style: A stylist working almost entirely with borrowed structures: desaturated colour, slow motion and ensemble posturing applied to plots taken from American and Korean originals.
historical_importance: Not a critical reputation, but his remake-led crime films and the two Shootout pictures are a distinct and commercially durable strand of 2000s Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: Two films five years apart and in different capacities. He directed and co-wrote Kaante (2002), a Reservoir Dogs remake shot in Los Angeles in which Bachchan leads a six-man ensemble as Major — recorded in this workbook as an ensemble lead, and a notable film of his comeback years for putting him among younger stars as an equal. He then produced and co-wrote Shootout at Lokhandwala (2007) with Suresh Nair and Apoorva Lakhia, in which Bachchan plays Advocate Dhingra in support, alongside Ekta Kapoor as co-producer; he also wrote lyrics for that film. Two of his collaborators there, Suresh Nair and Ekta Kapoor, are separately in this roster.
most_important_collaboration: Kaante (2002), which he directed and in which Bachchan leads the cast.
biography: Sanjay Gupta has built a thirty-year career on remaking foreign crime films for Hindi audiences: Kaante from Reservoir Dogs, Zinda from Oldboy, Jazbaa from Seven Days, and the Shootout films from documented Mumbai police encounters. His visual register — desaturated, slow, posed — is consistent enough to be recognisable, and he has cast Sanjay Dutt and John Abraham repeatedly. Kaante, in 2002, is the more interesting of his two Bachchan films: shot in Los Angeles with six male leads, it placed Bachchan among actors thirty years younger and treated him as one of the group rather than its patriarch. Shootout at Lokhandwala, which he produced and co-wrote in 2007, gave him a smaller part as a defence lawyer. Milap Zaveri wrote Kaante's dialogue and appears separately in this batch. His article had to be fetched under a pinned title, since a bare 'Sanjay Gupta' returns a different person, and it does not mention Bachchan. The entry is graded High.

name: Sanjeev Kohli
career_background: The son of the composer Madan Mohan, and chief executive of Yash Raj Films from 2000 to 2009. He is a music executive and archivist of his father's work rather than a working composer, and his most prominent credit is the reconstruction of unused Madan Mohan compositions. No birth date could be established.
debut: Not established as a composer; his defining credit is Veer-Zaara (2004).
major_works: Veer-Zaara (2004); Rann (2010); Chintamani (2014)
recurring_themes: The recovery and completion of his father's unrecorded music.
creative_style: Not a composer in the usual sense: on his principal credit he selected, arranged and completed existing melodies rather than writing new ones.
historical_importance: Veer-Zaara's soundtrack is among the most unusual in Hindi cinema — a hit album of new songs by a composer who had been dead for twenty-nine years — and it is his doing.
relationship_with_actor: Two films six years apart and very different in kind. Veer-Zaara (2004) is the significant one: Kohli found his father's unused recordings shortly after Madan Mohan's death in 1975, tested more than a hundred tunes, judged about thirty to fit, and finalised nine songs and two bonus tracks for Yash Chopra's film, in which Bachchan makes an extended special appearance. He is credited on Rann (2010) among a group of composers, in a film where Bachchan plays the lead, the television proprietor Vijay Harshvardhan Malik. The first credit connects directly to another entry in this roster, since Madan Mohan is recorded here as a collaborator on the strength of that same posthumous Veer-Zaara credit.
most_important_collaboration: Veer-Zaara (2004), the film on which his reconstruction of his father's music is the whole of his contribution.
biography: Sanjeev Kohli ran Yash Raj Films as chief executive from 2000 to 2009, and his lasting contribution to Hindi film music is an act of curation rather than composition. His father, Madan Mohan, died in 1975 leaving unused recordings, which Kohli preserved; for Veer-Zaara in 2004 he tested over a hundred of those tunes, selected about thirty as fitting the film, and completed nine songs and two bonus tracks, producing a successful album credited to a composer three decades dead. Madan Mohan appears separately in this roster on the strength of that same credit, so the two rows describe one posthumous collaboration from both sides — a structure repeated in this batch by S. D. Burman, whose songs were recreated for Chup in 2022. A critical sourcing caution is recorded: a direct Wikipedia fetch of 'Sanjeev Kohli' returns a Scottish actor born in 1971, an entirely different person, and that article was identified as wrong and discarded. No biography of this Sanjeev Kohli was located. The entry is graded Low.

name: Sapan Chakraborty
career_background: A composer, arranger, singer and lyricist in Hindi and Bengali films who came to prominence after joining R. D. Burman's team as an assistant music director. He composed for about five Hindi and fifteen Bengali films and wrote many of R. D. Burman's Bengali puja songs. No birth or death date could be established.
debut: Not established; Naya Nasha (1973) is the earliest of his credits located here.
major_works: Naya Nasha (1973); 36 Ghante (1974); Zameer (1975); and a larger body of Bengali film music
recurring_themes: Bengali melodic sensibility carried into Hindi film scoring, in the idiom of the R. D. Burman workshop where he trained.
creative_style: An arranger's composer, formed inside another composer's team, who also sang and wrote lyrics.
historical_importance: Not independently established; he is representative of the arrangers and assistants around R. D. Burman who occasionally composed in their own right.
relationship_with_actor: Two films two years apart, both from Bachchan's breakthrough period. He composed Naya Nasha (1973), on which Bachchan is only the narrator, and Zameer (1975), a B. R. Chopra production directed by Ravi Chopra in which Bachchan plays Badal Singh in the lead. Accounts of his career name Zameer, together with 36 Ghante, as the highlight of his work as a music director, which makes his second Bachchan film the peak of his own composing career.
most_important_collaboration: Zameer (1975), described in accounts of his career as one of the high points of his work as a composer.
biography: Sapan Chakraborty made his name inside R. D. Burman's team, where he worked as an assistant music director, arranger and singer, and he wrote many of Burman's Bengali puja songs as a lyricist. His own composing career was modest in Hindi — about five films — and much larger in Bengali, where he scored some fifteen. The two Hindi films counted here are Naya Nasha, where Bachchan narrates, and Zameer, where he plays the lead; a tribute article describes Zameer and 36 Ghande as the highlights of his work as a music director. He has no Wikipedia article, and the sources consulted, including a tribute framed around a death anniversary, did not give a year of birth or death, so both fields are left blank. R. D. Burman, whose team he joined, is PERSON-001 in this roster and its most frequent collaborator with thirty films, and C. J. Pavri, who wrote Zameer's story, is recorded in the previous batch. The entry is graded Low.

name: Saraswati Entertainment
career_background: Saraswati Entertainment Creations Limited, a production company that partners with larger houses rather than producing alone. No founding date, ownership or full slate could be established.
debut: Piku (2015) is the earliest credit located for the banner.
major_works: Piku (2015); Ghoomer (2023)
recurring_themes: Small, character-driven films made in partnership with Shoojit Sircar's and R. Balki's circles.
historical_importance: Not established. The banner is recorded because it carries the production credit on two films in this filmography.
relationship_with_actor: Two films eight years apart, and the first is among the most important of Bachchan's late career. On Piku (2015) the banner appears alongside MSM Motion Pictures and Rising Sun Films, and Bachchan plays Bhashkor Banerjee, the hypochondriac father who is both the comedy and the obstacle of the film — a co-lead, and the one late role in this filmography where a genuine romantic thread survives around him. On Ghoomer (2023) it appears alongside Hope Film Makers and Amitabh Bachchan Corporation, and he appears as himself. The banner's partners on both films are already in this roster.
most_important_collaboration: Piku (2015), one of the strongest performances of Bachchan's final phase.
biography: Saraswati Entertainment Creations Limited is a minority partner rather than a lead producer, and it is documented almost entirely through the two films that name it. On Piku it joined MSM Motion Pictures and Shoojit Sircar and Ronnie Lahiri's Rising Sun Films — the group responsible, with Juhi Chaturvedi's scripts, for the three strongest late Bachchan films, Piku, Pink and Gulabo Sitabo. On Ghoomer it appears with Hope Film Makers and Bachchan's own AB Corp. It has no Wikipedia article; searches confirmed only its Piku credit, and the Ghoomer credit rests on that film's wikitext studio field alone. No founding date, ownership or wider slate was located, so the row records what the two films establish and no more. The entry is graded Low.

name: Shaad Ali
career_background: Born 14 March 1975 in Kanpur to the director Muzaffar Ali and the politician Subhashini Ali, and a grandson of the Azad Hind Fauj commander Lakshmi Sahgal and Colonel Prem Sahgal; his paternal grandfather was the former ruling prince of Kotwara in Awadh, and he is a nephew of Kartikeya Sarabhai and Mallika Sarabhai. Educated at Welham Boys' School and the Lawrence School, Sanawar, he began as an assistant to Mani Ratnam on Dil Se.. (1998).
debut: Saathiya (2002), made for Yash Raj Films and Madras Talkies, a remake of Mani Ratnam's Alai Payuthey from a script by Ratnam.
major_works: Saathiya (2002); Bunty Aur Babli (2005); Jhoom Barabar Jhoom (2007); Kill Dil (2014); Ok Jaanu (2017); Soorma (2018)
recurring_themes: Young couples and the texture of modern courtship, handled with a strong emphasis on music and movement; several of his films are remakes of Mani Ratnam's.
creative_style: A Yash Raj house style crossed with Mani Ratnam's — glossy, song-driven, romance-centred film-making, at its most confident in his first two features.
historical_importance: Saathiya and Bunty Aur Babli were among the most popular Hindi romances of their years, and the latter is a landmark of casting rather than of direction.
relationship_with_actor: Two films two years apart, and the first is significant for a reason outside its own merits. Bunty Aur Babli (2005), which Ali directed, brought Amitabh Bachchan and Abhishek Bachchan together on screen for the first time as real-life father and son, alongside Rani Mukerji; Amitabh plays DCP Dashrath Singh, the policeman pursuing the pair, in a supporting role, and the film was one of the year's biggest hits. Jhoom Barabar Jhoom (2007) used him again, in an extended special appearance as a street musician who frames the film, once more opposite Abhishek Bachchan. Both credits place the father in the margins of his son's films.
most_important_collaboration: Bunty Aur Babli (2005), the first film to put Amitabh and Abhishek Bachchan on screen together.
biography: Shaad Ali comes from an unusually distinguished family — his father is the film-maker Muzaffar Ali, his mother the Communist politician Subhashini Ali, and his grandparents Lakshmi Sahgal and Prem Sahgal of the Indian National Army — and learned the trade as Mani Ratnam's assistant. His first two films were his best received: Saathiya, a remake of Ratnam's Alai Payuthey scripted by Ratnam himself, and Bunty Aur Babli, which is remembered less for its small-town con-artist plot than for casting Amitabh Bachchan as the policeman chasing a couple played by his own son and Rani Mukerji, the first time father and son had appeared together. Jhoom Barabar Jhoom followed in 2007, with the older Bachchan reduced to a framing appearance as a street musician. His later films were poorly received. One incidental connection runs to the previous batch: his article records that he briefly dated Pooja Shetty, daughter of the Adlabs founder Manmohan Shetty, whose production subsidiary is PERSON-151. The entry is graded High.

name: Shaktimaan Talwar
career_background: A Hindi film writer active in the mid-2000s. No biographical detail, birth date or wider career could be established; searches returned only his film credits.
debut: Not established; Ab Tumhare Hawale Watan Saathiyo (2004) is the earliest of his credits located here.
major_works: Ab Tumhare Hawale Watan Saathiyo (2004); Family: Ties of Blood (2006)
recurring_themes: Patriotic and family melodrama of the kind Anil Sharma and the Ramsay-produced commercial cinema of the period traded in.
historical_importance: Not established. He is recorded because he is a credited writer on two films in this filmography.
relationship_with_actor: Two films two years apart, both with substantial Bachchan roles. He is the sole credited writer of Ab Tumhare Hawale Watan Saathiyo (2004), Anil Sharma's long patriotic drama in which Bachchan plays Major General Amarjeet Singh in support of a large cast. He then wrote the story of Family: Ties of Blood (2006) with Ashok Raut, in which Bachchan plays Virendra Sahai, the gangster antagonist — one of the few outright villain roles of his later career. The two are unusual for a writer of this obscurity in giving the actor a general and a crime boss rather than peripheral parts.
most_important_collaboration: Family: Ties of Blood (2006), where Bachchan plays the antagonist and the story is Talwar's own.
biography: Shaktimaan Talwar is credited as the writer of Ab Tumhare Hawale Watan Saathiyo (2004) and as co-author of the story of Family: Ties of Blood (2006), and almost nothing else about him could be established: he has no Wikipedia article, and no birth date, death date or further filmography was located. The two films themselves are well documented. The first is Anil Sharma's three-hour patriotic drama, in which Bachchan appears as an army officer; the second is Rajkumar Santoshi's gangster film, produced by Keshu Ramsay under DMS Films — both separate entries in the previous batch — in which Bachchan plays the villain against Akshay Kumar. On Ab Tumhare Hawale the wikitext credits him alone in the writer field, and on Family it credits the story to him with Ashok Raut. The entry is graded Low.

name: Sheel Kumar
career_background: A producer working with Shoojit Sircar and Ronnie Lahiri's Rising Sun Films. No birth date or biographical detail could be established; he is documented through the films he has produced.
debut: Not established; Pink (2016) is the earliest credit located here.
major_works: Pink (2016); Gulabo Sitabo (2020)
recurring_themes: The Rising Sun register — small-cast, character-led films rooted in a specific Indian city, several of them written by Juhi Chaturvedi.
historical_importance: Not independently established, but he is a producing hand on two of the strongest films of Bachchan's final phase.
relationship_with_actor: Two films four years apart, and both are among the best late Bachchan roles. On Pink (2016) he is named among the producers in the film's own awards citations — its Filmfare Best Film nomination at the 62nd Filmfare Awards and its AACTA Best Asian Film nomination credit Rashmi Sharma, Pawan Kumar, Shoojit Sircar and Sheel Kumar — and Bachchan plays Deepak Sehgall, the reclusive lawyer who takes on a sexual-assault case, as co-lead. On Gulabo Sitabo (2020), which he produced with Ronnie Lahiri, Bachchan plays Mirza under heavy prosthetics, the mercenary landlord waiting to outlive his much older wife; that film carries the only romance row in the last fifty films of this filmography. For a two-film producer, the quality of the pair is exceptional.
most_important_collaboration: Gulabo Sitabo (2020), where his producing credit is primary rather than shared among four, and which gives Bachchan the more extraordinary of the two performances.
biography: Sheel Kumar produces for Rising Sun Films, the company Shoojit Sircar and Ronnie Lahiri founded in 2007, and his two credits here belong to the group that gave Bachchan the strongest run of his last two decades: Piku, Pink and Gulabo Sitabo, all made by the same circle and two of them written by Juhi Chaturvedi. On Pink he is one of four producers named in the film's awards citations; on Gulabo Sitabo he produced with Ronnie Lahiri. Bachchan is a co-lead in both — a lawyer coming out of seclusion in the first, a grasping Lucknow landlord in the second — and Gulabo Sitabo supplies PAIR-095, the single romance row in the final fifty films of this workbook. He has no Wikipedia article, and no birth date or career history was located; his Pink credit is documented through that film's awards tables rather than its infobox. Rising Sun Films, Shoojit Sircar, Ronnie Lahiri and Juhi Chaturvedi are all separate entries in this roster. The entry is graded Low.

name: Sippy Films
career_background: The production banner of G. P. Sippy, established after the modest success of his first film, Sazaa (1951). Born in Karachi into a Sindhi Hindu trading family and trained as a lawyer, Sippy moved to Mumbai at Partition in 1947; he was president of the IMPPA in 1965–66 and of the Film Federation of India across four terms between 1972 and 1992. In 2026 the company secured outside investment and repositioned itself as a character-IP-led studio built on its legacy titles.
debut: Sazaa (1951) preceded the banner; the company was established on its success.
major_works: Brahmachari (1968); Andaz (1971); Seeta Aur Geeta (1972); Sholay (1975); Shaan (1980); Saagar (1985)
recurring_themes: Large-scale commercial entertainment made at the top of the market, most of it directed by his son Ramesh Sippy.
creative_style: A producer's house in the fullest sense: it spent heavily, shot long, and backed its director's ambition, which is how Sholay came to be made on the scale it was.
historical_importance: The banner behind Sholay, the most commercially successful and most widely quoted Hindi film ever made, and behind Shaan and Saagar.
relationship_with_actor: Two films five years apart, and the first is the single most important commercial film in this filmography. Sholay (1975), directed by Ramesh Sippy and written by Salim–Javed, casts Bachchan as Jai opposite Dharmendra's Veeru, a co-lead that became the defining friendship of Hindi cinema and ends in his death; the film is credited to United Producers and Sippy Films and was distributed by Sippy Films. Shaan (1980), also directed by Ramesh Sippy, cast him as Vijay Kumar in an ensemble attempt to repeat the formula, and did not. The banner therefore accounts for both the peak of the Sippy–Bachchan association and the film that showed it could not be reproduced.
most_important_collaboration: Sholay (1975), by common consent the most significant commercial Hindi film ever made, and a defining Bachchan role.
biography: Sippy Films was G. P. Sippy's company, founded on the strength of his first production, Sazaa, in 1951, and it became one of the dominant houses of the 1970s. Sippy himself came from a Sindhi trading family in Karachi, trained as a lawyer, moved to Bombay at Partition and went on to lead both the IMPPA and the Film Federation of India across two decades. The banner's summit is Sholay, directed by his son Ramesh Sippy from a Salim–Javed script, in which Bachchan plays Jai; Shaan followed in 1980 with much the same team and a fraction of the effect. The company was still trading in 2026, when it took investment to relaunch as a character-IP studio built on its own library. It has no Wikipedia article of its own — the Sholay wikitext pipes its name to G. P. Sippy's article and the Shaan wikitext uses a link that resolves to nothing. Both G. P. Sippy and Ramesh Sippy are already in this roster, and this workbook records the Sippys as two unrelated families, the other being N. C. and Romu Sippy. The entry is graded Medium.

name: Sneha Khanwalkar
career_background: Born 28 April 1983 in Indore, an Indian music director working in Hindi films and active from 2004. She is known for field-recording and folk-sourced methods, which she also made the subject of the television series Sound Trippin.
debut: Composing from 2004; her breakthrough was Oye Lucky! Lucky Oye! (2008).
major_works: Oye Lucky! Lucky Oye! (2008); Gangs of Wasseypur Parts 1 and 2 (2012); Ghoomketu (2020); Chup: Revenge of the Artist (2022); the series Sound Trippin
recurring_themes: Regional and folk idioms recorded on location and built into film songs, in deliberate opposition to studio-made soundtracks.
creative_style: A field recordist as much as a composer: she collects voices and instruments in the places a film is set and assembles songs from them, which gives her soundtracks an unpolished, specific quality.
major_awards: Nominated for Best Music Director at the 58th Filmfare Awards for Gangs of Wasseypur, becoming only the second woman nominated in that category, 28 years after Usha Khanna.
historical_importance: One of the very few women to have composed for mainstream Hindi cinema and the second ever nominated for the Filmfare Best Music Director award, and the most prominent practitioner of location-sourced film music in India.
relationship_with_actor: Two films two years apart, in both of which Bachchan appears as himself. She composed songs for Ghoomketu (2020), a COVID-era streaming release, sharing the soundtrack with Jasleen Royal — so that film pairs the two women composers in this batch. She then worked on Chup: Revenge of the Artist (2022), where she is credited alongside Amit Trivedi and S. D. Burman, and specifically with recreating Burman's songs; Bachchan again appears as himself. That recreation credit links her row directly to PERSON-206, and makes her the second person in this batch, after Sanjeev Kohli on Veer-Zaara, to be credited for completing a dead composer's work.
most_important_collaboration: Chup: Revenge of the Artist (2022), where her recreation of S. D. Burman's songs is the substance of the credit.
biography: Sneha Khanwalkar composes by going out and recording: her method, made explicit in her television series Sound Trippin, is to gather voices and instruments in the region a film inhabits and build songs from that material, and it produced the soundtracks of Oye Lucky! Lucky Oye! and Gangs of Wasseypur, for which she was nominated for the Filmfare Award for Best Music Director — only the second woman ever nominated in the category, 28 years after Usha Khanna. Her two credits in this filmography are late and small in Bachchan's terms, since he appears as himself in both, but they are interesting in themselves. On Ghoomketu she shares the soundtrack with Jasleen Royal, the other woman composer in this batch; on Chup she is credited with recreating S. D. Burman's songs for a film about Guru Dutt, whose own films Burman had scored — a posthumous collaboration forty-seven years after his death, and the exact counterpart of Sanjeev Kohli's work on Veer-Zaara recorded in this same batch. The entry is graded High.

name: Sohel Don
career_background: Nothing is known of his life or training. He surfaces in the mid-1980s as one of several dialogue writers on Manmohan Desai's productions and leaves no trace outside three credits.
debut: Not established. His earliest located credit is Mard (1985).
major_works: Mard (1985); Allah-Rakha (1986); Gangaa Jamunaa Saraswathi (1988)
recurring_themes: Late-period Manmohan Desai masala: filial duty, disguise, mother-worship and declamatory confrontation scenes.
creative_style: No source describes his writing. In both films counted here he is one name in a composite dialogue credit rather than the sole author of the script.
major_awards: None located.
historical_importance: Marginal. He is of interest only as a member of the Desai writing room, which the workbook now documents in some depth.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both Manmohan Desai's and both with Bachchan in the lead, at the two ends of Desai's decline. Mard (1985) was the last enormous hit of the Desai–Bachchan partnership; Gangaa Jamunaa Saraswati (1988) was the flop that effectively ended it. On Mard he shares the writing credit with Prayag Raj, Pushpa Raj Anand, Inder Raj Anand, Anil Nagrath and K. K. Shukla, and on Gangaa Jamunaa Saraswati with Kader Khan, Anil Nagrath, Prayag Raj and K. K. Shukla. There is no evidence of direct contact with Bachchan.
most_important_collaboration: Mard (1985), the larger film and the bigger commercial success.
biography: Sohel Don is one of the least documented people in this roster: no Wikipedia article, no birth or death date, no interview, no obituary, and a total of three located credits, all of them dialogue work on Manmohan Desai films between 1985 and 1988. He belongs to the house writing team the workbook has already traced through K. K. Shukla (PERSON-011), Desai's principal writer, and Prayag Raj (PERSON-018); Desai's scripts were assembled by committee, and Don's name appears inside composite credits alongside four or five others on each film. Because both of his credits fall in Bachchan's lead years under Desai, he is attached to two of the most-seen films of the period while remaining personally invisible. The entry is graded Low and rests on a search-result summary plus the two film articles.

name: SPE Films India
career_background: The Indian film production and distribution arm of Sony Pictures Entertainment. Sony had produced in India before, but relaunched its local production business in 2018, and the two films counted here are that relaunch slate.
debut: As relaunched: Pad Man and 102 Not Out, both 2018.
major_works: Pad Man (2018); 102 Not Out (2018)
recurring_themes: Mid-budget, socially themed Hindi films with major stars — a menstrual-hygiene campaigner's biography and a comedy about extreme old age — aimed at a wide domestic audience rather than at the multiplex margins.
creative_style: A studio financier and distributor rather than a creative house; both films were developed by their Indian producers and boarded by Sony.
major_awards: None located for the banner itself.
historical_importance: A case of a Hollywood major producing local-language Indian films directly rather than distributing imports. Variety's 2021 reporting frames the unit as nurturing local talent while expanding Sony's Hollywood footprint.
relationship_with_actor: Two films released three months apart in 2018, and they use Bachchan in opposite registers. In Pad Man (February) he is only the off-screen narrator; in 102 Not Out (May) he is the co-lead, playing a 102-year-old father opposite Rishi Kapoor's 75-year-old son, the pair's first film together in 27 years. Variety reported Sony boarding 102 Not Out specifically as a Bachchan–Kapoor vehicle, so the star pairing was the reason for the investment.
most_important_collaboration: 102 Not Out (2018), where the banner is the lead producer and Bachchan the lead actor.
biography: SPE Films India is Sony Pictures Entertainment's Indian production arm, and its identification here required unpicking a wrong-entity trap. A Wikipedia fetch under the name returns Sony Pictures Networks India, a 26-channel television conglomerate — a sibling Sony company, not this banner — and the two film wikitexts pipe the display name to two different targets, Culver Max Entertainment in one and Sony Pictures Networks in the other, which by the rule established in batch 4 means neither target is the entity. The banner itself has no article. What is documented is the 2018 relaunch of Sony's local Indian production business, of which Pad Man and 102 Not Out were the opening pair. On Pad Man it is one of six banners and Bachchan merely narrates; on 102 Not Out it is the lead producer and Bachchan plays the title role. The entry is graded Low because it rests on trade reporting reached through a web search rather than on any dedicated account of the company.

name: Sunanda Murali Manohar
industry: Tamil, Hindi, British and American cinema
career_background: Born Sunanda Mandre on 10 September 1957, an Indian-British producer and entrepreneur based in London who produced with her husband, the ENT surgeon Dr J. Murali Manohar. Her output spans Tamil, Hindi, Kannada, British and American films across nearly three decades. In 2001 she launched South for You, a south Indian Tamil channel on Britain's Sky network, running it until she sold it in 2011, after which UTV took it over. She died on 30 December 2017.
debut: Indian Summer (British, 1987).
major_works: Jeans (1998); Jodi (1999); Minnale (2001); Majnu (2002); Arasatchi (2003); Ramji Londonwaley (2005); Provoked (2006); Dhaam Dhoom (2008); Kochadaiiyaan (2014)
recurring_themes: Tamil commercial cinema and diaspora-facing English-language films, often shot or set in Britain.
creative_style: A transnational producer who financed Tamil films for the overseas market and English-language films about Indians abroad, working from London rather than Chennai or Mumbai.
major_awards: None located.
historical_importance: One of the few women running an independent transnational production and broadcasting business between India and Britain in this period; the Sky channel gave Tamil-language programming a national British platform for a decade.
relationship_with_actor: Two films nine years apart, and in neither does Bachchan play a character. In Ramji Londonwaley (2005), a Hindi remake of a Tamil film about an Indian cook in London — squarely her territory — he appears as himself. In Kochadaiiyaan (2014), Soundarya Rajinikanth's motion-capture animated film, he narrates the Hindi version. Both are uses of his public persona rather than his acting, which is characteristic of how late-career producers deployed him.
most_important_collaboration: Kochadaiiyaan (2014), the far larger production and her last film.
biography: Sunanda Murali Manohar was an Indian-British producer who built an unusual career between London and Chennai. With her husband she produced across five languages and three national industries, from Tamil hits such as Minnale and Jeans to British and American titles including Provoked and Blood Stone, and in 2001 she launched a Tamil channel on Sky that she ran for a decade. Her two Bachchan credits are both films that use him without casting him: he appears as himself in Ramji Londonwaley, a London-set comedy that matches her own diasporic subject matter, and narrates the Hindi version of Kochadaiiyaan, the Rajinikanth motion-capture epic that proved to be her last production. She died in December 2017, three years after it was released. The entry is graded Medium: her article is well populated with a filmography but carries no career narrative, and it never mentions Bachchan.

name: Sunil Manchanda
career_background: An Indian producer and director who came from advertising production, where he worked as an ad-film producer before moving into features. He produces through the banner Mad Entertainment.
debut: Not established from the sources; his earliest feature credit located here is Tere Naam (2003).
major_works: Tere Naam (2003); Cheeni Kum (2007); Paa (2009)
recurring_themes: Small-cast, single-premise films built around one performance, made cheaply enough that an unconventional subject is not a commercial risk.
creative_style: The producer of R. Balki's early films, backing a director whose material — a 64-year-old chef courting a 34-year-old woman, a boy with progeria played by a 67-year-old star — would have been unfinanceable at a larger scale.
major_awards: The article records that Paa won five awards from 14 nominations at the 16th Star Screen Awards and that Cheeni Kum won one award and received four nominations including the Apsara Award for Best Movie (2008); these are the films' awards, not his personally.
historical_importance: Modest in himself, but he financed the two films that opened Bachchan's late character-lead phase under a first-time director.
relationship_with_actor: Two consecutive R. Balki films with Bachchan at the centre of both, and between them they define his late career. Cheeni Kum (2007) casts him as a cantankerous London chef in a romance with a woman thirty years younger; Paa (2009) casts him, under heavy prosthetics, as a twelve-year-old boy with progeria whose father is played by his own son Abhishek, a role that won Bachchan the National Film Award for Best Actor. On Paa he co-produces with Bachchan and Abhishek Bachchan directly, so the relationship there is a working partnership rather than a hiring.
most_important_collaboration: Paa (2009), Bachchan's most-awarded late performance.
biography: Sunil Manchanda is an advertising producer turned film producer whose importance to this filmography is out of all proportion to his three-sentence Wikipedia article. Through Mad Entertainment he backed R. Balki's first two features, Cheeni Kum and Paa, both built entirely around Bachchan and both premised on an idea a cautious financier would refuse: an old man's romance in the first, and in the second a 67-year-old playing a dying child opposite his real son as the father. Paa brought Bachchan his fourth National Film Award for Best Actor and was co-produced with the Bachchans themselves. His banner, Mad Entertainment, is PERSON-178 in this roster with the same two films, so producer and banner are the same collaboration counted twice — the sixth such pair the workbook has recorded. The article itself carries no birth date, no career narrative and no mention of Bachchan, so the entry is graded Medium and leans on the two film articles.

name: Swanand Kirkire
career_background: Born in Indore, Madhya Pradesh, a lyricist, playback singer, screenwriter, dialogue writer, assistant director, actor and author working in Hindi and Marathi film and television since 2003. He is best known as a lyricist but maintains a parallel career as a dialogue writer, and has acted in films and web series, including Panchayat 3 and Qala.
debut: Hazaaron Khwaishein Aisi (2003) as a lyricist.
major_works: As lyricist: Parineeta (2005); Lage Raho Munna Bhai (2006); 3 Idiots (2009). As writer: Eklavya: The Royal Guard (2007); Pad Man (2018). As actor: Chumbak (2018)
recurring_themes: Plain, colloquial Hindi carrying moral argument — songs and dialogue that sound spoken rather than written, often for films with an explicit social thesis.
creative_style: A writer of demotic Hindustani who moves between lyric and dialogue; his best-known songs work as argument set to music, and his dialogue work is hired for the same quality.
major_awards: National Film Award for Best Lyrics twice — 2006 for 'Bande Me Tha Dum...Vande Mataram' from Lage Raho Munna Bhai and 2009 for 'Behti Hawa Sa Tha Woh' from 3 Idiots — and the National Film Award for Best Supporting Actor at the 66th National Film Awards for the Marathi film Chumbak. Nominated for the Filmfare Award for Best Lyrics for 'Piyu Bole' from Parineeta (2005).
historical_importance: One of the most decorated Hindi lyricists of his generation, with three National Film Awards across two entirely different crafts.
relationship_with_actor: Two films eleven years apart, and in both he is a writer rather than a lyricist — a distinction worth making, since it is his lyric work that is famous. On Eklavya: The Royal Guard (2007) he shares the writing credit with Vidhu Vinod Chopra and Abhijat Joshi for a film built on Bachchan's near-wordless performance as a royal bodyguard losing his sight. On Pad Man (2018) he shares the screenplay with R. Balki, on a film in which Bachchan only narrates. There is no evidence of direct contact.
most_important_collaboration: Eklavya: The Royal Guard (2007), where Bachchan plays the title role and the writing is central to it.
biography: Swanand Kirkire is that rare figure who has won National Film Awards in two unrelated crafts — twice for lyrics, for Lage Raho Munna Bhai and 3 Idiots, and once for acting, for the Marathi film Chumbak. He is in this roster, though, for neither: both of his Bachchan credits are writing jobs, on Eklavya: The Royal Guard and Pad Man, and his article maintains a separate 'As dialogue writer' section that documents this second career. His verse is colloquial and argumentative, and the same plainness is what directors hire his dialogue for. His article contradicts itself on his birth year, giving 29 April 1970 in the infobox against 29 April 1972 in the lead, so no birth year is recorded here. He also appears in the Sye Raa Narasimha Reddy credits as a lyricist, a film outside his two counted collaborations. The entry is graded High.

name: T. Rama Rao
career_background: Born Tatineni Rama Rao on 29 May 1938 at Kapileswarapuram in the Madras Presidency, he directed 75 Hindi and Telugu feature films between 1966 and 2000 and also worked as a producer. He died in Chennai on 20 April 2022.
debut: Directing from 1966; his Hindi career belongs to the late 1970s and the 1980s.
major_works: Andha Kanoon (1983); Inquilaab (1984); Aakhree Raasta (1986, through his banner)
recurring_themes: Vigilante justice and institutional corruption, with a wronged man forced outside the law — a template he moved between Telugu and Hindi with the cast changed.
creative_style: A high-volume professional who worked fast across two industries, remaking proven southern material for the Hindi market with northern stars.
major_awards: None located; his article records no awards.
historical_importance: One of the most prolific of the Telugu directors who colonised Hindi cinema in the 1980s, a traffic that reshaped the decade's commercial films.
relationship_with_actor: Two films a year apart at a particular moment: Andha Kanoon (1983) is the film Bachchan shot around his recovery from the Coolie injury, and Rajinikanth's Hindi debut, with Bachchan in an extended special appearance rather than the lead. Inquilaab (1984) gives him the lead as a policeman turned political killer.
