Outside that credit nothing about him could be found — no Wikipedia article, no birth date, no second film — and even his name is unstable, appearing as Jiji Philip in the film's own wikitext and Jijy Philip in database listings. His inclusion in this roster is an artifact of how anthology films distribute credits: Bachchan's scenes belong to the frame narrative, which Varma directed, so the two never worked together. The workbook records the relationship as nominal rather than implying a collaboration that did not occur. Graded Low.

name: K. Bhagyaraj
career_background: Born Krishnaswamy Bhagyaraj on 7 January 1953 at Vellankoil near Gobichettipalayam and died in Chennai on 27 June 2026. A filmmaker, actor, musician and politician who worked predominantly in Tamil cinema, he began in the mid-1970s as an assistant director under G. Ramakrishnan and Bharathiraja, wrote scripts and dialogue while taking small acting roles, and from the early 1980s directed films in which he usually played the lead. He wrote and directed more than 25 films, acted in over 75, edited the Tamil weekly Bhagya and wrote several novels. His son is the actor Shanthanu.
debut: Directing from the early 1980s, after an apprenticeship with Bharathiraja.
major_works: Mouna Geethangal; Darling Darling Darling; Chinna Veedu; Aakhree Raasta (1986); Rasukutty
recurring_themes: Rural and small-town Tamil life, marriage and its discontents, and comedy grounded in social embarrassment; he frequently remade his own films in other languages.
creative_style: A writer-director-star in the fullest sense, controlling script, direction and lead performance, with a reputation as one of the most influential writer-directors in 1980s Tamil cinema.
major_awards: None located in the article.
historical_importance: Among the most influential Tamil writer-directors of the 1980s, and a significant conduit of Tamil material into Hindi cinema through remakes.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and its casting is documented. Bhagyaraj set out in 1985 to direct a Hindi remake of Bharathiraja's 1984 film Oru Kaidhiyin Diary, with Rajesh Khanna in the lead; Khanna dropped out over dates, and Bhagyaraj cast Amitabh Bachchan instead. The result was Aakhree Raasta (1986), in which Bachchan plays David D'Costa in a double role as father and son, one of his most admired performances of the decade. The film was produced by A. Poornachandra Rao for Lakshmi Productions of Madras, the banner associated with T. Rama Rao (PERSON-231).
most_important_collaboration: Aakhree Raasta (1986), his only film with Bachchan.
biography: K. Bhagyaraj was one of the dominant writer-directors of Tamil cinema in the 1980s, a Bharathiraja protégé who wrote, directed and starred in his own films, acted in more than seventy others, edited a weekly magazine and wrote novels. He directed one Hindi film, Aakhree Raasta, a remake of Bharathiraja's Oru Kaidhiyin Diary, and his article records exactly how Bachchan came to it: Rajesh Khanna was cast first, in 1985, and dropped out over scheduling, at which point Bhagyaraj turned to Bachchan. The film gave Bachchan a double role as a wronged father and his policeman son and is among the strongest performances of his mid-career. Bhagyaraj died on 27 June 2026, less than three months before this research date; his article's infobox repeats the birth date in the death field, so the lead's dates are used. Graded High.

name: K. V. Raju
career_background: Born in 1954, a director, screenwriter and dialogue writer who worked in Kannada and Hindi cinema. He entered the Kannada industry in 1982 as associate director on Baadada Hoo, directed by his brother K. V. Jayaram, and made his own debut as director and scriptwriter with Olave Baduku (1984), going on to direct many acclaimed Kannada films through the 1980s and 1990s. He died of a heart attack at his Rajajinagar home in Bengaluru on 24 December 2021, aged 67.
debut: Olave Baduku (1984) in Kannada; Indrajeet (1991) in Hindi.
major_works: Olave Baduku (1984); Indrajeet (1991); Udhaar Ki Zindagi; Khooni Jung
recurring_themes: Not characterised in the sources; his Hindi films are action and melodrama.
creative_style: No source describes his direction in detail.
major_awards: None located.
historical_importance: A respected Kannada director of the 1980s and 1990s whose three-film Hindi career is the smaller part of his work.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it was his entry into Hindi cinema. Indrajeet (1991) casts Bachchan as Inspector Indrajeet, produced by Ramesh Behl for Rose Audio Visuals with music by R. D. Burman, and Raju co-wrote it with Kader Khan as well as directing. His article names the film explicitly as his Hindi debut, which is what confirms the identification against a common name. The film came in the weak commercial stretch before Bachchan's 1992 retreat from acting.
most_important_collaboration: Indrajeet (1991), his only film with Bachchan.
biography: K. V. Raju was a Kannada director who came up through his brother K. V. Jayaram's films, debuted with Olave Baduku in 1984 and built a solid reputation in Kannada cinema across two decades. He directed three Hindi films, the first of which was Indrajeet (1991), with Amitabh Bachchan as a police inspector, produced by Ramesh Behl and scored by R. D. Burman; Raju shared the writing with Kader Khan. It belongs to the run of unsuccessful early-1990s films that preceded Bachchan's five-year withdrawal from acting. Raju died of a heart attack in Bengaluru in December 2021. His article does not mention Bachchan, but it names Indrajeet as his Hindi debut, which was decisive in confirming this is the right K. V. Raju and not the economist of the same name. Graded High.

name: Kaizad Gustad
career_background: Born in Bombay in 1968, a director and author based in Mumbai. He has written three books — Of No Fixed Address, published by HarperCollins in 1998, The Road to Mandalay and 7 Storeys — alongside his film work.
debut: Bombay Boys (1998).
major_works: Bombay Boys (1998); Boom (2003)
recurring_themes: Diaspora Indians colliding with Bombay, told in English-language or heavily English-inflected films with an outsider's eye and a taste for the seedy.
creative_style: An English-language independent sensibility applied to Bombay subjects; Bombay Boys was among the first Indian films aimed squarely at that register.
major_awards: None located.
historical_importance: Bombay Boys was an early and influential English-language Indian independent film. His article also carries an 'Incidents' section, indicating controversy attached to his career.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it is among the most notorious in this filmography. Boom (2003) is a black-comedy thriller in which Bachchan plays Bade Mia, a crime boss — an outright antagonist role, rare for him — alongside Zeenat Aman, Jackie Shroff, Gulshan Grover and Javed Jaffrey, with the models Padma Lakshmi, Madhu Sapre and Katrina Kaif as the female leads, making their film debuts. Kaif's career began here. The film was a critical and commercial disaster.
most_important_collaboration: Boom (2003), his only film with Bachchan.
biography: Kaizad Gustad made Bombay Boys in 1998, an English-language independent film about three diaspora Indians adrift in Bombay that was influential out of proportion to its size, and he has published three books. His second feature, Boom, is his only credit in this filmography and one of the strangest entries in Bachchan's career: a black-comedy thriller about stolen diamonds in which Bachchan plays the gangster Bade Mia opposite Zeenat Aman, Jackie Shroff and Gulshan Grover, with three supermodels — Padma Lakshmi, Madhu Sapre and Katrina Kaif — as the leads. It was savaged on release and is now remembered chiefly as Katrina Kaif's debut. His article carries an 'Incidents' section not summarised here. Graded High for the biography, though the article is short.

name: Kangana Ranaut
career_background: Born Kangna Amardeep Ranaut in Mandi, Himachal Pradesh, on 23 March 1986, an actress, filmmaker and politician, and Member of Parliament for Mandi since June 2024. She modelled briefly at sixteen, trained in acting under the theatre director Arvind Gaur, and made her film debut in the thriller Gangster (2006). She has won four National Film Awards and four Filmfare Awards, appeared six times in the Forbes India Celebrity 100 list, and received the Padma Shri in 2020.
debut: As actress, Gangster (2006); as director, Manikarnika: The Queen of Jhansi (2019).
major_works: As actress: Woh Lamhe... (2006); Life in a... Metro (2007); Fashion (2008); Queen; Tanu Weds Manu Returns. As director: Manikarnika: The Queen of Jhansi (2019); Emergency
recurring_themes: Strong-willed, unconventional women in female-led films; as a director, nationalist historical and political subjects.
creative_style: As a director she works in the register of the patriotic historical epic, with herself in the title role.
major_awards: Four National Film Awards and four Filmfare Awards, including the Filmfare Award for Best Female Debut for Gangster; Padma Shri (2020). These are overwhelmingly for acting, not directing.
historical_importance: One of the most prominent and most publicly contentious figures in Hindi cinema of her generation, and since 2024 a sitting Member of Parliament.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and she is in this roster only as its director, not as its star. She took over the direction of Manikarnika: The Queen of Jhansi (2019) from Krish Jagarlamudi during production and shares the director credit with him; she also plays Rani Lakshmibai. Bachchan does not appear in the film — he narrates it. There is no documented working contact between them, and her 183 KB article does not mention him once.
most_important_collaboration: Manikarnika: The Queen of Jhansi (2019), her only film in this filmography.
biography: Kangana Ranaut is one of the most decorated actresses of her generation, with four National Film Awards, four Filmfare Awards and the Padma Shri, and since 2024 the Member of Parliament for Mandi. She enters this roster in an unexpected capacity: as a director. During the making of Manikarnika: The Queen of Jhansi she took over direction from Krish Jagarlamudi, who is PERSON-268 in this same batch, and the two share the credit; she also plays the Rani. Bachchan's contribution is the narration, so the collaboration is between a performer he never shared a scene with and a voice recorded separately. Her article is the longest fetched in this batch and never mentions him. The entry is graded High for the biography, with the collaboration recorded as narration only.

name: Khwaja Ahmad Abbas
career_background: Born in Panipat, Punjab, on 7 June 1914 and died in Bombay on 1 June 1987. A film director, screenwriter, novelist and journalist working in Urdu, Hindi and English, active for more than fifty years. In 1951 he founded his own production company, Naya Sansar, through which he made socially engaged films including Anhonee, Munna, Rahi (1953), from a Mulk Raj Anand story about tea-plantation workers, Shehar Aur Sapna and Saat Hindustani.
debut: Working in film from 1935; Dharti Ke Lal (1946) was his first major film as director.
major_works: As director: Dharti Ke Lal (1946); Pardesi (1957); Shehar Aur Sapna (1963); Saat Hindustani (1969); Do Boond Pani (1972). As screenwriter: Neecha Nagar (1946); Awaara (1951); Jagte Raho (1956)
recurring_themes: Famine, poverty, labour, communal unity and national integration — a body of work organised around social justice and the idea of India.
creative_style: A neo-realist and a pioneer of Indian parallel cinema, committed to social subjects taken from reportage; he was a working journalist throughout and wrote fiction alongside his films.
major_awards: Four National Film Awards; the Palme d'Or at Cannes for a film he wrote, from three nominations; the Crystal Globe at Karlovy Vary for Jagte Raho (1957), which also took a Certificate of Merit at the fourth National Film Awards; National Film Award for Best Feature Film for Shehar Aur Sapna (1963); National Film Awards for Best Feature Film on National Integration for Saat Hindustani (1969) and Do Boond Pani (1972); BFJA Best Screenplay for Naya Sansar (1942); a Cannes nomination for Pardesi (1958).
historical_importance: One of the founders of Indian parallel and neo-realist cinema, the writer of Awaara and Jagte Raho, and the maker of Dharti Ke Lal, one of the first Indian social-realist films, which opened the Soviet market to Indian cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it is the beginning of everything. Saat Hindustani (1969) is Amitabh Bachchan's screen debut: Abbas cast him, an unknown, as Anwar Ali, one of seven Indians of different communities who set out to liberate Goa from the Portuguese. The film won the National Film Award for Best Feature Film on National Integration. This workbook's entry for Tinnu Anand (PERSON-068) records that Anand was the assistant sent to offer the unknown Bachchan ₹5,000 for the part. Abbas never worked with him again, and his article names the film repeatedly without ever naming Bachchan.
most_important_collaboration: Saat Hindustani (1969), Bachchan's first film.
biography: Khwaja Ahmad Abbas was a journalist, novelist and filmmaker whose work runs through the whole first half-century of Indian cinema: he wrote Awaara and Jagte Raho for Raj Kapoor, made Dharti Ke Lal about the Bengal famine, won four National Film Awards, and had films at Cannes and Karlovy Vary. He is one of the founders of Indian parallel cinema and among the few Indian filmmakers of his era with a genuine international reputation. His single connection to this filmography is decisive: he gave Amitabh Bachchan his first role, casting him as Anwar Ali in Saat Hindustani, a film about seven men of different faiths and regions trying to free Goa, which won the National Film Award for Best Feature Film on National Integration in 1969. Bachchan was unknown and was hired for ₹5,000, a detail this workbook records through Tinnu Anand, the assistant who carried the offer. Abbas's infobox is malformed, with the birth place in the birth-date field and the birth date in the death field, so all dates are taken from the lead. Graded High.

name: Krish Jagarlamudi
career_background: Born Radhakrishna Jagarlamudi in Guntur, Andhra Pradesh, on 10 November 1978 and known as Krish, a director and screenwriter working predominantly in Telugu cinema. He has won a National Film Award and two Filmfare Awards South.
debut: Gamyam (2008).
major_works: Gamyam (2008); Vedam (2010); Vaanam (2011); Krishnam Vande Jagadgurum (2012); Kanche (2015); Gabbar Is Back (2015); Gautamiputra Satakarni (2017); Manikarnika: The Queen of Jhansi (2019); NTR: Kathanayakudu and NTR: Mahanayakudu (2019)
recurring_themes: Historical and period subjects, hyperlink narratives and biographical drama, with a recurring interest in caste and social division.
creative_style: A director of large-scale period films who also works in multi-strand contemporary narratives; his period work is built on scale and declamation.
major_awards: A National Film Award — his 2015 period war drama Kanche won the National Film Award for Best Feature Film in Telugu — and two Filmfare Awards South.
historical_importance: One of the leading Telugu directors of period and biographical epics in the 2010s.
relationship_with_actor: One film, which he did not finish. He began directing Manikarnika: The Queen of Jhansi (2019) and left during production; its star Kangana Ranaut took over and the two share the director credit. Bachchan narrates the film and does not appear in it. His article lists Manikarnika among his works without noting that he departed, and never mentions Bachchan.
most_important_collaboration: Manikarnika: The Queen of Jhansi (2019), his only film in this filmography.
biography: Krish Jagarlamudi is among the most prominent Telugu directors of the 2010s, with the National Film Award for Best Telugu Feature Film for Kanche, two Filmfare Awards South, and a body of work running from the road film Gamyam and the hyperlink drama Vedam to the period epics Gautamiputra Satakarni and the two-part NTR biography. His one credit here is Manikarnika: The Queen of Jhansi, which he began and did not complete — Kangana Ranaut, its star, took over the direction, and the two are credited together; she is PERSON-266 in this same batch, so a single divided directing job produced two roster rows. Bachchan's involvement is the narration, recorded separately from either director's work. His article lists the film among his credits and passes over the handover in silence. Graded High for the biography.

name: Leena Yadav
career_background: Born on 6 January 1971, a director, producer, screenwriter and editor who began in television and moved into features. She is married to the cinematographer Aseem Bajaj.
debut: Shabd (2005).
major_works: Shabd (2005); Teen Patti (2010); Parched (2015); Rajma Chawal (2018)
recurring_themes: Women's constrained lives and the cost of leaving them; Parched, her best-known film, follows four women in rural Rajasthan.
creative_style: A director who came up through editing and television, working in intimate character drama; Parched premiered internationally and is the film her reputation rests on.
major_awards: None located in the article.
historical_importance: Parched, her first international feature, premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2015 and is among the more widely travelled Indian films about women's lives of its decade.
relationship_with_actor: One film. Teen Patti (2010) casts Bachchan as Professor Venkat Subramanium, a mathematician who devises a system for beating the odds at cards and takes his students to the gambling tables, opposite Ben Kingsley. Yadav directed, co-wrote and supplied the story. It was not a success, and it is one of the few Bachchan films directed by a woman.
most_important_collaboration: Teen Patti (2010), her only film with Bachchan.
biography: Leena Yadav came to directing through television and editing, and is best known for Parched, her study of four women in rural Rajasthan, which premiered at Toronto in 2015. Her other features are Shabd, Rajma Chawal and Teen Patti, the last of which is her only credit in this filmography: Bachchan plays a mathematics professor who applies probability theory to gambling and is drawn into the consequences, with Ben Kingsley opposite him. She directed it, co-wrote it and wrote the story. The film failed, but the credit is notable for a different reason — very few films in this roster of 306 collaborators were directed by a woman, and Yadav is one of only a handful. Her article is short and mentions neither Teen Patti nor Bachchan, so the credit rests on the film's own article. Graded Medium.

name: Mahesh Manjrekar
career_background: Born Mahesh Vaman Manjrekar in Mumbai on 16 August 1958 and active since 1975, an actor, director, screenwriter and producer working primarily in Hindi, Marathi and Telugu films. He hosted the Marathi edition of the reality show Bigg Boss and is a member of the Maharashtra Navnirman Sena. His daughter is the actress Saiee Manjrekar.
debut: Directing with Vaastav: The Reality (1999).
major_works: Vaastav: The Reality (1999); Astitva (2000); Viruddh... Family Comes First (2005); as actor, Kaante (2002) and many others
recurring_themes: Ordinary Maharashtrian families broken by violence, crime or moral failure; the decent man pushed past endurance.
creative_style: A performer's director who writes and acts as well, drawing heavily on Marathi theatre and on middle-class Mumbai settings, with a taste for confrontation played at full pitch.
major_awards: A National Film Award, seven Maharashtra State Film Awards, four Filmfare Awards Marathi, a Filmfare Award, four Zee Chitra Gaurav Puraskar, four MFK Awards and two Star Screen Awards; the V. Shantaram Award, Maharashtra's highest cinema honour, in 2023. His awards tables list Astitva for Best Feature Film in Marathi at the National Film Awards (2000), Vaastav for Filmfare Best Director and Best Scene of the Year and IIFA Best Director, and Kaante for Filmfare and IIFA Best Comedian, with every Result cell blank.
historical_importance: A leading figure in the revival of Marathi cinema and, with Vaastav, the director of one of the defining Hindi gangster films of the late 1990s.
relationship_with_actor: One directing credit, but the two men worked together twice. He directed Viruddh... Family Comes First (2005), in which Bachchan plays Vidhyadhar Patwardhan, a retired Maharashtrian pensioner who turns on the powerful family that murdered his son — one of the strongest late-career performances, produced by Bachchan's own ABCL. Three years earlier Manjrekar had acted alongside him in Kaante, for which his own article records Filmfare and IIFA nominations as Best Comedian. The writers of Viruddh, Yash-Vinay (PERSON-244), had also written Kaante, so the connection between the two films runs through both director and writers.
most_important_collaboration: Viruddh... Family Comes First (2005), the film he directed and one of Bachchan's best late roles.
biography: Mahesh Manjrekar is an actor, writer and director whose Vaastav: The Reality (1999) is among the defining Hindi gangster films of its moment and whose Astitva won the National Film Award for Best Feature Film in Marathi; he has since become a central figure in Marathi cinema and received the V. Shantaram Award in 2023. His one directing credit here, Viruddh... Family Comes First, is a domestic revenge drama in which Bachchan plays a mild retired Maharashtrian man who destroys the family that killed his son, made by Bachchan's own company ABCL and widely regarded as one of his finest late performances. The two had already shared the screen in Kaante, where Manjrekar acted, and the writing duo Yash-Vinay carried over from that film to this one. Every Result cell in all four of his awards tables is blank, so no win is asserted from them and the counts given are the article's own claim. Graded High.

name: Milan Luthria
career_background: Born Milan Arjun Luthria in Mumbai on 28 January 1968 and directing since 1999, he works in Hindi films and is best known for the period gangster drama Once Upon a Time in Mumbaai (2010) with Ajay Devgn.
debut: Kachche Dhaage (1999).
major_works: Kachche Dhaage (1999); Chori Chori (2003); Deewaar (2004); Taxi No. 9211 (2006); Once Upon a Time in Mumbaai (2010); The Dirty Picture (2011)
recurring_themes: Men bound by codes of loyalty — smugglers, brothers, soldiers — often set in a stylised past.
creative_style: A commercial director with a taste for period texture and male ensembles, working repeatedly with Ajay Devgn.
major_awards: His awards table lists Best Director nominations for Once Upon a Time in Mumbaai at the BIG Star Entertainment, Screen, Stardust, Lions Gold, Zee Cine, Apsara and IIFA awards; every Result cell is blank, so no win is asserted.
historical_importance: Once Upon a Time in Mumbaai revived the Bombay-underworld period film in the 2010s.
relationship_with_actor: One film. Deewaar (2004) — no relation to the 1975 film of the same title — casts Bachchan as an Indian Army major captured by the Pakistani army during the 1971 war along with more than thirty soldiers, and held for 33 years until his son mounts a rescue; Sanjay Dutt and Akshaye Khanna co-star. The role is a co-lead built almost entirely on stillness and confinement, and it belongs to the run of films in which the older Bachchan plays fathers whose sons come for them.
most_important_collaboration: Deewaar (2004), his only film with Bachchan.
biography: Milan Luthria has directed Hindi commercial films since 1999, from Kachche Dhaage through Taxi No. 9211 to Once Upon a Time in Mumbaai, the 2010 gangster period piece that is his best-known work and that restarted a whole cycle of Bombay-underworld films. His single credit in this filmography is Deewaar (2004), a prisoner-of-war drama that shares nothing but its title with the 1975 Deewaar also in this workbook: Bachchan plays a major taken prisoner in the 1971 war and left in a Pakistani jail for 33 years, with Sanjay Dutt and Akshaye Khanna, and his son eventually comes to get him out. It is a confined, largely reactive performance quite unlike the roles the earlier Deewaar made him famous for. Luthria's article records a long row of Best Director nominations for Once Upon a Time in Mumbaai with every result cell left blank, so none is claimed here. The entry is graded High.

name: Mukul Dutt
career_background: A Hindi film director whose located credits run from 1970 to 1973. IMDb indexes him under the Music Department as well as Director and Second Unit or Assistant Director, suggesting a working career broader than the three films that can be confirmed.
debut: Not established; his earliest located credit is Aan Milo Sajna (1970).
major_works: Aan Milo Sajna (1970); Raaste Kaa Patthar (1972); Chhalia (1973)
recurring_themes: Early-1970s commercial melodrama; too little is documented to characterise the work.
creative_style: No source describes his direction.
major_awards: None located.
historical_importance: Slight in the record, though his abandoned project is a curiosity in its own right.
relationship_with_actor: One counted film and one uncounted, and the uncounted one is the more interesting. Raaste Kaa Patthar (1972) is a comedy drama written by Rahi Masoom Reza and Jayant Dharmadhikari, with Bachchan alongside Shatrughan Sinha and Prem Chopra, released on 1 December 1972 in the pre-Zanjeer period when Bachchan was taking whatever work came. Separately, Yaar Meri Zindagi (FILM-194) records that its shooting began in 1976 under Mukul Dutt, who left in 1984 after 'numerous problems and creative differences'; Ashok Gupta finished it in 1998 and it was released in 2008. So Dutt began a second Bachchan film and walked away from it after eight years, and the roster counts only the one he completed.
most_important_collaboration: Raaste Kaa Patthar (1972), the only film of his that reached release with Bachchan in it.
biography: Mukul Dutt directed Raaste Kaa Patthar in 1972, a comedy drama with Amitabh Bachchan, Shatrughan Sinha and Prem Chopra written by Rahi Masoom Reza, and is otherwise barely documented: no Wikipedia article, no birth or death date, and only two other confirmed credits, Aan Milo Sajna and Chhalia. His second involvement with this filmography is the one worth recording. He began shooting Yaar Meri Zindagi in 1976 and left the production in 1984 after protracted disagreements; Ashok Gupta (PERSON-249) took it over in 1998, finished it within a year, and it finally reached about twenty screens in 2008 — a 32-year span in which Dutt occupied the first eight. The frozen roster counts him for one film, and the abandoned one carries Gupta's name. Jayant Dharmadhikari, his co-writer on Raaste Kaa Patthar, is PERSON-164. Graded Low.

name: Nag Ashwin
career_background: Born Singireddy Nag Ashwin Reddy on 23 April 1986, a director and screenwriter in Telugu cinema and a graduate of the New York Film Academy. He began as an assistant director to Sekhar Kammula and has won two National Film Awards, a Nandi Award and a Filmfare Award.
debut: Yevade Subramanyam (2015), which won him the Nandi Award for Best Debut Director.
major_works: Yevade Subramanyam (2015); Mahanati (2018); Kalki 2898 AD (2024)
recurring_themes: Ambitious formal departures from Telugu commercial convention — a coming-of-age road film, a period biopic of an actress, a science-fiction epic drawn from the Mahabharata.
creative_style: A director who changes register completely between films and works at increasing scale, with a strong interest in Indian mythology reframed through genre.
major_awards: National Film Award for Best Feature Film in Telugu and the Filmfare Award for Best Director – Telugu for Mahanati (2018); Nandi Award for Best Debut Director for Yevade Subramanyam; Kalki 2898 AD won Best Production Design and Best Popular Feature Film at the 72nd National Film Awards.
historical_importance: Mahanati became the highest-grossing female-led South Indian film, and Kalki 2898 AD is among the largest science-fiction productions attempted in India.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and commercially it is the biggest of Bachchan's life. In Kalki 2898 AD (2024) he plays Ashwatthama, the cursed immortal of the Mahabharata, in a co-lead alongside Prabhas, Deepika Padukone and Kamal Haasan; the film grossed around ₹1,180 crore worldwide, by a wide margin the highest figure in this filmography. Collider's review, quoted in the article, praised the film as a 'unique sci-fi epic' with strong performances by Prabhas and Bachchan. At 81 he was cast as a warrior of the Mahabharata in a film set in 2898.
most_important_collaboration: Kalki 2898 AD (2024), his only film with Bachchan and Bachchan's highest-grossing film.
biography: Nag Ashwin has made three features in nine years and no two resemble each other: Yevade Subramanyam, a coming-of-age road film that won him a Nandi Award; Mahanati, a biopic of the actress Savitri that became the highest-grossing female-led South Indian film and brought him the National Film Award for Best Telugu Feature Film; and Kalki 2898 AD, a dystopian science-fiction epic that transplants the Mahabharata into the year 2898. The last of these is his only point of contact with this filmography and it is a substantial one — Bachchan plays Ashwatthama, the immortal cursed to walk the earth, opposite Prabhas, and the film is the highest-grossing of his entire career, taking roughly ₹1,180 crore worldwide at the age of 81. The film won two National Film Awards at the 72nd ceremony. Graded High.

name: Nagraj Manjule
career_background: Born Nagraj Popatrao Manjule on 24 August 1978 in Jeur, Maharashtra, a director, actor, producer, scriptwriter and poet working in Marathi cinema. In 2018 he published a Marathi poetry collection, Unhachya Katavirudhha, which won the Bhairuratan Damani Sahitya Puraskar.
debut: The short film Pistulya, which won the National Film Award for Best Debut Film of a Director (non-feature); his first feature was Fandry (2013).
major_works: Pistulya (2010); Fandry (2013); Sairat (2016); Pavsacha Nibandh (2017); Jhund (2022)
recurring_themes: Caste. His films are among the most direct treatments of caste oppression in Indian cinema — a Dalit boy's humiliation in Fandry, an inter-caste romance destroyed in Sairat, slum youth excluded from institutions in Jhund.
creative_style: A realist who casts non-professionals from the communities he films, works in rural and small-town Maharashtra, and refuses the consolations of the commercial ending.
major_awards: National Film Award for Best Debut Film of a Director (non-feature) for Pistulya at the 58th National Film Awards; the Indira Gandhi Award for Best Debut Film of a Director for Fandry at the 61st; National Film Award for Best Director in Non-Feature Film for Pavsacha Nibandh at the 65th; Filmfare Marathi Best Director for Fandry and for Sairat, and the Zee Chitra Gaurav Puraskar for Sairat.
historical_importance: The most significant figure in Marathi cinema of his generation, and the director who took an unsparing account of caste to a mass Indian audience with Sairat.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it is his Hindi debut. Jhund (2022) casts Bachchan as Vijay Borade, a retiring sports teacher who builds a football team out of slum children — a character modelled on the real Vijay Barse and his organisation Slum Soccer. The article states twice that Manjule's Hindi debut was Jhund starring Amitabh Bachchan. It is one of the late roles in which Bachchan's authority is used against the grain, as an institutional figure arguing for people the institution excludes.
most_important_collaboration: Jhund (2022), his only film with Bachchan.
biography: Nagraj Manjule is the leading Marathi director of his generation and the most uncompromising chronicler of caste in contemporary Indian cinema. Pistulya, Fandry and Sairat won him National Film Awards and, in Sairat's case, an enormous popular audience for a film that ends in an honour killing. Jhund, his Hindi debut, is his only film in this filmography: Bachchan plays a retiring sports teacher who assembles a football team from the slum children the city has written off, a role based on the real-life founder of Slum Soccer. Casting the most established star in Hindi cinema inside a Manjule film is an unusual move for both, and the result places Bachchan's authority at the service of the director's subject rather than the other way round. He is also a poet, with a prize-winning Marathi collection. Graded High.

name: Nitesh Tiwari
career_background: Born on 22 May 1973 in Itarsi, Madhya Pradesh, a director, screenwriter and lyricist in Hindi cinema, active since 2011. He co-founded Earthsky Pictures, which produces advertising films and the docu-series Break Point. He is married to the filmmaker Ashwiny Iyer Tiwari.
debut: Chillar Party (2011), as co-writer and co-director.
major_works: Chillar Party (2011); Bhoothnath Returns (2014); Dangal (2016); Chhichhore (2019)
recurring_themes: Children and young people pushed to achieve, and the adults who drive or fail them; institutions — schools, hostels, sport — examined from the inside.
creative_style: Broad, emotionally legible storytelling with a strong comic register, built on ensembles of young performers and a clear moral argument.
major_awards: Two National Film Awards for Chillar Party (Best Children's Film and Best Screenplay); the Filmfare Award for Best Director at the 62nd Filmfare Awards and the Telstra People's Choice Award at the 2017 Indian Film Festival of Melbourne for Dangal; a third National Film Award, for Best Feature Film in Hindi, for Chhichhore. His awards table also lists a Filmfare Best Dialogue entry for Bhoothnath Returns.
historical_importance: Dangal is the highest-grossing Indian film, with an enormous Chinese theatrical run, and Tiwari is among the most commercially successful directors in the industry.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it was his first as sole director. Bhoothnath Returns (2014) casts Bachchan as the ghost Kailash Nath, who returns from the afterlife and stands for election against a corrupt politician — a children's fantasy sequel that turns into a film about voting. It is one of the few late Bachchan films with a lead role built for a young audience. Tiwari made Dangal two years later; his article does not mention Bachchan at all.
most_important_collaboration: Bhoothnath Returns (2014), his solo directorial debut.
biography: Nitesh Tiwari came out of advertising into film as co-writer and co-director of Chillar Party, which won two National Film Awards, and then made Bhoothnath Returns as his first solo feature — the only film of his in this filmography, with Bachchan as a ghost who contests an election against a corrupt politician and campaigns for the right to vote. Two years later he wrote and directed Dangal, which became the highest-grossing Indian film ever made and won him the Filmfare Award for Best Director, and in 2019 Chhichhore brought him a third National Film Award. His films are built around young ensembles and a plainly stated moral case, which is exactly what Bhoothnath Returns does with its children's-fantasy premise. His article never mentions Bachchan despite the star carrying his solo debut. Graded High.

name: O. P. Goyle
career_background: Nothing has been established about him beyond a single directing credit. No birth date, no training and no second film could be located.
debut: Not established.
major_works: Bandhe Haath (1973)
recurring_themes: Not determinable from one film.
creative_style: No source describes his direction.
major_awards: None located.
historical_importance: Negligible personally, but the film he directed holds a small first in Bachchan's career.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it matters more than its obscurity suggests. Bandhe Haath (1973), produced and written by O. P. Ralhan, is the first film in which Amitabh Bachchan played a dual role — a device that would recur through Don, Adalat, Kasme Vaade, The Great Gambler, Satte Pe Satta, Aakhree Raasta and Sooryavansham. Bachchan plays Shyamu, a pickpocket who takes on a dead writer's identity. On release the film found no takers; after Zanjeer made Bachchan a star later the same year it drew renewed interest, recovered its cost and finished as average.
most_important_collaboration: Bandhe Haath (1973), his only film with Bachchan.
biography: O. P. Goyle directed Bandhe Haath, released in February 1973, and is otherwise absent from the record — no Wikipedia article, no birth or death date, no other credit. The film is worth more attention than he can be given: it is the first of Amitabh Bachchan's many double roles, and its commercial history is a neat illustration of what Zanjeer did to him. Released before that breakthrough, Bandhe Haath found no buyers; once Bachchan became a star a few months later, the same film drew an audience, recovered its cost and was rated average. Goyle should not be confused with O. P. Ralhan, the film's producer and writer and a substantially better-documented figure, whose name differs by two letters. Graded Low, on a search summary and the film's own article.

name: Prakash Verma
career_background: Nothing has been established. No article, no birth date, no second credit; the name is common enough that a Wikipedia fetch was deliberately pinned to a title expected to miss rather than risk returning a different person.
debut: Not established.
major_works: Bansi Birju (1972)
recurring_themes: Not determinable from one film.
creative_style: No source describes his direction.
major_awards: None located.
historical_importance: None established.
relationship_with_actor: One film, from the period before either of its stars was famous. Bansi Birju (1972), released on 1 September 1972, pairs Amitabh Bachchan with Jaya Bhaduri: Bansi is an orphaned village girl sold into an ashram in Bombay who escapes and is hidden and protected by Birju, and the two fall in love. It belongs with Ek Nazar and Sanjog among the Bachchan–Bhaduri films made before their marriage in June 1973, when both were working actors rather than stars.
most_important_collaboration: Bansi Birju (1972), his only film with Bachchan.
biography: Prakash Verma directed Bansi Birju in 1972, a romance in which Amitabh Bachchan protects and falls in love with a young woman who has escaped from the ashram she was sold to as a child, played by Jaya Bhaduri. Beyond that credit the record holds nothing: no article, no dates, no other film, and a name too common to search safely, so the Wikipedia fetch was pinned to a title expected to return nothing rather than risk attaching the wrong person's biography to this row. The film's interest is its place in the sequence of Bachchan–Bhaduri pairings — Ek Nazar, Bansi Birju, Sanjog and others — made in the eighteen months before they married and before Zanjeer separated his career from hers. Graded Low.

name: Pramod Chakravorty
career_background: Born in Calcutta on 15 August 1929 and died in Mumbai on 12 December 2004, an Indian Hindi film producer and director active across more than four decades, from 1955 to 1998.
debut: Directing from the mid-1950s; his article gives no titles in the fetched extract.
major_works: Nastik (1983) is the only title confirmed from the sources used here.
recurring_themes: Not characterised by any source located.
creative_style: No source describes his direction.
major_awards: None recorded in the article.
historical_importance: A long professional career as producer-director, but one that the available sources describe only in outline.
relationship_with_actor: One film. Nastik (1983) casts Bachchan as Shankar, a man whose faith is destroyed by a corrupt godman and who turns against religion before being drawn back — a lead role in one of the run of 1983 films released around the Coolie accident. The workbook records no Romances row for Nastik, the sources being too thin to describe the relationship honestly. Chakravorty's article does not mention Bachchan or the film.
most_important_collaboration: Nastik (1983), his only film with Bachchan.
biography: Pramod Chakravorty worked as a Hindi film producer and director for over forty years, from 1955 to 1998, and died in Mumbai in 2004. That is very nearly all his Wikipedia article says: the lead is a single sentence, the fetched extract yields no film titles, no account of his style and no awards, and the infobox repeats his birth date in the death field. His single credit in this filmography is Nastik (1983), in which Bachchan plays a man whose belief is broken by a fraudulent holy man. Given how thin the record is, this row deliberately claims little: a long career is documented, its contents are not. Graded Medium — the dates and the fact of the career are reliable, the substance is absent.

name: Prawaal Raman
career_background: An Indian director and screenwriter in Hindi cinema who emerged from the Ram Gopal Varma stable in the early 2000s and has written and directed his own films since 2003.
debut: Darna Mana Hai (2003).
major_works: Darna Mana Hai (2003); Gayab (2004); Darna Zaroori Hai (2006); 404 (2011); Main Aur Charles (2015)
recurring_themes: Horror and psychological unease, twice in portmanteau form; his later work turns to true crime with Main Aur Charles, about the criminal Charles Sobhraj.
creative_style: A genre director trained in the Varma school's low-budget, high-concept method, comfortable with anthology structure.
major_awards: None located.
historical_importance: Darna Mana Hai and Darna Zaroori Hai are the two films that established the portmanteau horror format in 2000s Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and they share no scene. Darna Zaroori Hai (2006) is a six-story horror portmanteau with seven credited directors; Raman directed one segment, having also directed the earlier Darna Mana Hai. Bachchan appears only in the frame narrative, as Professor Sunil Khanna, the schoolteacher telling the tales, which Ram Gopal Varma directed. The credit is shared, the work is not.
most_important_collaboration: Darna Zaroori Hai (2006), his only film in this filmography.
biography: Prawaal Raman came up through Ram Gopal Varma's company and made his name with Darna Mana Hai in 2003, the portmanteau horror film that established the format in Hindi cinema; he returned to it for Darna Zaroori Hai in 2006, directing one of its six stories. That film is his only credit here, and it is one of three rows in this roster — with Jiji Philip and J. D. Chakravarthy in batch 6, and Vivek Shah and Sajid Khan in this one — generated by a single anthology in which Bachchan's scenes belong to the frame story that Varma himself directed. His later films moved away from horror, notably Main Aur Charles, about Charles Sobhraj. His article is short, gives no birth date and does not mention Bachchan. Graded Medium.

name: Puri Jagannadh
career_background: Born Petla Jagannadh on 28 September 1966 in Pithapuram, Andhra Pradesh, a director, screenwriter and producer working primarily in Telugu cinema. He produces through Puri Jagannadh Touring Talkies, Vaishno Academy and Puri Connects, the last co-owned with the actress Charmme Kaur, and owns a music company, Puri Sangeet.
debut: Badri (2000), with Pawan Kalyan, Renu Desai and Ameesha Patel.
major_works: Badri (2000); Itlu Sravani Subramanyam; Appu; Idiot; Pokiri (2006); Bbuddah... Hoga Terra Baap (2011)
recurring_themes: Swaggering male heroes, street dialogue and mass-appeal action; Pokiri's undercover-cop premise became one of the most remade plots in Indian cinema.
creative_style: A writer-director of star vehicles with a distinctive ear for colloquial dialogue, working fast and at high volume.
major_awards: None recorded in the article.
historical_importance: Pokiri premiered at the 7th IIFA Film Festival in Dubai and was remade into several Indian languages, making him one of the most influential Telugu commercial directors of the 2000s.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it is a knowing star vehicle. Bbuddah... Hoga Terra Baap (2011) casts Bachchan as Vijay Malhotra, an ageing gangster who returns to Mumbai, and plays throughout on the audience's memory of his own 1970s persona — the title is a line of self-mockery about being old. It was produced by Abhishek Bachchan with Viacom18 and ABCL. Puri Jagannadh's article records that he worked with Amitabh Bachchan on it and that the film was archived in the Oscar library, which is a print acceptance rather than any award or nomination.
most_important_collaboration: Bbuddah... Hoga Terra Baap (2011), his only film with Bachchan.
biography: Puri Jagannadh is one of the most prolific Telugu commercial directors of the last quarter-century, with Badri, Idiot and above all Pokiri — a film remade across several Indian languages — to his name, alongside production companies and a music label. He made his Hindi debut in 2004 with Shart: The Challenge, and his one film in this filmography is Bbuddah... Hoga Terra Baap, a 2011 vehicle built entirely around Bachchan's own iconography: an old gangster walking back into Mumbai, with a title that translates the joke about his age into a boast. Abhishek Bachchan produced it with Viacom18 and ABCL, so the film is a family project as much as a studio one. The article's claim that it was 'archived in the Oscar library' is repeated here only as the article's own, since it denotes a print being accepted into the Academy's library and not a nomination. Graded High.

name: Raj Khosla
career_background: Born Desraj Khosla on 31 May 1925 at Rahon, Punjab, and died in Bombay on 9 June 1991. He was among the leading directors, producers and screenwriters in Hindi cinema from the 1950s to the 1980s, beginning his career under Guru Dutt. His early background in classical music meant most of his films excelled in their music.
debut: Directing from 1949; his breakthrough was C.I.D. (1956).
major_works: C.I.D. (1956); Woh Kaun Thi? (1964); Mera Saaya (1966); Do Raaste (1969); Mera Gaon Mera Desh (1971); Main Tulsi Tere Aangan Ki (1978); Dostana (1980)
recurring_themes: Mystery and suspense with a supernatural suggestion, and melodramas structured around women's choices.
creative_style: Known for bringing neo-noir and visual style to Indian cinema and as a 'women's director' who showed actresses at their best; he, Guru Dutt and Vijay Anand were inspired by the Hitchcock school of mystery-suspense thrillers, and his films are notable for their songs.
major_awards: Main Tulsi Tere Aangan Ki won the Filmfare Award for Best Film; he was nominated for Filmfare Best Director for Do Raaste and for Main Tulsi Tere Aangan Ki.
historical_importance: One of the defining stylists of Hindi cinema's classical period, and the director most associated with the Indian suspense thriller.
relationship_with_actor: One film, made at the end of Khosla's run of success. Dostana (1980) casts Bachchan as Vijay Verma, a police inspector whose lifelong friendship with a lawyer, played by Shatrughan Sinha, is destroyed by their both loving the same woman, played by Zeenat Aman — a co-lead in a triangle that is as much about the two men as about her. His article records that after big hits like Main Tulsi Tere Aangan Ki and Dostana with Bachchan, Zeenat Aman and Shatrughan Sinha, Khosla ran into rough weather as his later films began to flop.
most_important_collaboration: Dostana (1980), his only film with Bachchan and one of his last hits.
biography: Raj Khosla began under Guru Dutt and became one of the great stylists of Hindi cinema, credited with importing neo-noir into the industry and known as a 'women's director' for the parts he wrote and the performances he drew from actresses — C.I.D., Woh Kaun Thi?, Mera Saaya, Mera Gaon Mera Desh, and Main Tulsi Tere Aangan Ki, which won the Filmfare Award for Best Film. A classical musician by training, he made films whose songs outlived their plots. His single Bachchan film, Dostana (1980), is a friendship-and-rivalry triangle with Shatrughan Sinha and Zeenat Aman, and his own article marks it as the last of his big successes before his fortunes turned. Vijay Anand, named in the same sentence of that article as a fellow Hitchcock admirer, is PERSON-300 in this batch. The infobox repeats his birth date in the death field, so dates come from the lead. Graded High.

name: Raj N. Sippy
career_background: Born Raj Sippy in Bombay on 6 March 1948, a director and producer of Hindi films, prominent through the 1980s and working until about 2010.
debut: Directing from 1978.
major_works: Inkaar; Satte Pe Satta (1982); Satyamev Jayate; Mahaadev; Boxer; Baazi; Thanedaar; Saugandh
recurring_themes: Star-driven action and crime films, several built around an actor's comeback or debut.
creative_style: A commercial director who worked repeatedly with Vinod Khanna and Mithun Chakraborty and was trusted with launch and comeback vehicles.
major_awards: None recorded in the article.
historical_importance: Notable as the director of several career-defining moments for other actors — Vinod Khanna's comeback in Satyamev Jayate and Akshay Kumar's debut in Saugandh.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it is one of the most enjoyable of Bachchan's career. Satte Pe Satta (1982) casts him as Ravi Anand, eldest of seven uncouth brothers whose lives are civilised by the woman he marries, and in a second role as the assassin Babu — a double part in a film loosely derived from Seven Brides for Seven Brothers. The workbook records separate Romances rows for the two characters. His article names the film among his successes of the 1980s.
most_important_collaboration: Satte Pe Satta (1982), his only film with Bachchan.
biography: Raj N. Sippy directed Hindi commercial films from 1978 to about 2010 and was at his most prominent in the 1980s, with Inkaar, Satyamev Jayate and Mahaadev for Vinod Khanna, Boxer and Baazi for Mithun Chakraborty, Thanedaar with Sanjay Dutt and Jeetendra, and Akshay Kumar's debut, Saugandh. His single Bachchan film is Satte Pe Satta, the 1982 musical comedy of seven brothers transformed by a new wife, in which Bachchan plays both the eldest brother and a murderous lookalike — one of the double roles that recur across his filmography and one of his lightest performances. His article does not say which of the two unrelated Sippy families in this roster he belongs to; the patronymic initial suggests the N. C. Sippy line rather than G. P. Sippy's, but no source located confirms it, so the connection is left open. Graded High.

name: Rakesh Roshan
career_background: Born Rakesh Roshan Nagrath in Bombay on 6 September 1949, a member of the Roshan film family, he appeared in 84 films in the 1970s and 1980s, mostly in supporting roles in big-budget productions, before turning to direction in 1987. Since then his films have all carried titles beginning with the letter K. In 2025 Netflix released a four-part documentary series about him.
debut: As director, Khudgarz (1987).
major_works: Khudgarz (1987); Khoon Bhari Maang (1988); Karan Arjun (1995); Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai (2000); Koi... Mil Gaya (2003); the Krrish series (2006–13)
recurring_themes: Family melodrama and revenge, and from 2003 a home-grown science-fiction and superhero franchise built around his son Hrithik Roshan.
creative_style: A producer-director who builds long-running franchises and has managed his son's career as closely as his own films; his work is unabashedly mainstream and structurally conservative.
major_awards: Filmfare Awards for Best Film and Best Director for Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai and for Koi... Mil Gaya. He was honoured at the International Film Festival of India in Panaji on 3 December 2006 and at the Global Indian Film Awards on 11 December 2006 for his contribution to Indian cinema.
historical_importance: Creator of the Krrish series, the first sustained Indian superhero franchise, and the architect of one of Hindi cinema's most successful star launches.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and Bachchan is only heard in it. Krrish 3 (2013) uses him as the narrator, framing the superhero story; he does not appear on screen. Roshan directed, produced, co-wrote and supplied the story. His article does not mention Bachchan, and the collaboration is a voice credit on a franchise film belonging entirely to the Roshan family.
most_important_collaboration: Krrish 3 (2013), his only film in this filmography.
biography: Rakesh Roshan acted in 84 films before he directed one, and has since built a career on two things: titles beginning with K, and his son. From Khudgarz and Khoon Bhari Maang through Karan Arjun to Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai — which launched Hrithik Roshan and won Roshan the Filmfare Awards for Best Film and Best Director — and then Koi... Mil Gaya and the Krrish films, he created the first durable Indian superhero franchise. His one credit in this filmography is the third of those, Krrish 3, where Bachchan supplies the opening narration and never appears. It is among the most peripheral collaborations in the roster, and his article, thorough about his own career and his son's, does not mention Bachchan once. Graded High for the biography, with the collaboration recorded as narration only.

name: Ramanjit "Tony" Juneja
career_background: Born Ramanjit Singh Juneja in Punjab, the son of a liquor supplier to Army canteen stores who owned warehouses in Nagaland, and the brother of the producer Kushaljeet 'Tito' Juneja. He changed his name to Tony Juneja for his film work. The brothers began by producing Assamese films in Guwahati, moved to Bombay and worked at Roop Tara Studios, and launched their banner Navjeevan Films in the 1970s.
debut: Not established as a director; the brothers' first production was Do Anjaane (1976).
major_works: As a producing partner: Do Anjaane (1976); Mr. Natwarlal (1979); Ram Balram (1980). As director: Insaniyat (1994)
recurring_themes: The family firm's output is Bachchan-dependent star melodrama and action.
creative_style: No source describes his direction; his single directing credit came at the end of the brothers' run, when their production business was already in decline.
major_awards: None located.
historical_importance: Slight as a director. His significance is as one half of the producing partnership that first paired Bachchan with Rekha.
relationship_with_actor: One directing credit, but the family relationship with Bachchan is much older. Insaniyat (1994), which he directed and his brother produced under Navjeevan Films, was released on 11 March 1994 with an ensemble of Amitabh Bachchan, Sunny Deol, Jaya Prada, Raveena Tandon and Chunky Panday; it came in the weakest commercial stretch of Bachchan's career. The brothers had produced Do Anjaane (1976), Mr. Natwarlal (1979) and Ram Balram (1980) with him before that, and DNA records that they drifted away from films as his popularity waned.
most_important_collaboration: Insaniyat (1994), his only directing credit with Bachchan.
biography: Tony Juneja, born Ramanjit Singh Juneja, is the younger half of the producing partnership behind Navjeevan Films, which he ran with his brother Kushaljeet 'Tito' Juneja — PERSON-234 in this roster. Together they produced Do Anjaane, the film that first put Amitabh Bachchan and Rekha on screen together, then Mr. Natwarlal and Ram Balram, before a long tail of failures. This row exists for his one directing credit, Insaniyat (1994), an ensemble film with Bachchan and Sunny Deol made near the end of the brothers' working life and of Bachchan's first career. Identifying him also closed a reconciliation opened in batch 6: the producer credited as 'Tito' on two films and 'Tito Juneja' on this one is a single person, so the frozen roster understates his brother's count. Neither brother has a Wikipedia article, and no birth or death dates were found for either. Graded Low.

name: Ravikant Nagaich
career_background: Born at Atrauli, Aligarh, in the United Provinces on 5 July 1931 and died in Madras on 6 January 1991. He began as a cinematographer in Telugu films, his first being N. T. Rama Rao's Sri Seetha Rama Kalyanam in 1961, and turned to Hindi films and direction with Farz.
debut: As director, Farz — a low-budget James Bond-inspired thriller that was a surprise hit and lifted the careers of its leads, Jeetendra and Babita.
major_works: Farz; Mere Jeevan Saathi; The Train; Keemat (1973); Surakksha; Wardat; Raksha (1982); Duty (1986)
recurring_themes: The Indian secret-agent film. He returned repeatedly to the Agent 116 character — Dharmendra played him in Keemat, Jeetendra in Raksha and The Gold Medal.
creative_style: A cinematographer-turned-director who worked cheaply and fast; his best-remembered films are the low-budget spy pictures, recalled as much for their tacky stunts and special effects as in spite of them.
major_awards: None located.
historical_importance: The principal exponent of the Indian James Bond imitation, a small but distinct genre of the late 1960s and 1970s.
relationship_with_actor: One film, from the very start of Bachchan's career. Pyar Ki Kahani (1971) is among his earliest credits, made when he was an unknown taking whatever was offered, two years before Zanjeer. Nagaich's article does not mention Bachchan or the film, and no account of their working relationship exists.
most_important_collaboration: Pyar Ki Kahani (1971), his only film with Bachchan.
biography: Ravikant Nagaich shot Telugu films before he directed Hindi ones, and made his name with Farz, a cheap James Bond imitation that became a surprise hit and turned Jeetendra into a star. He spent much of his career on that formula, returning to the Agent 116 character across Keemat, Raksha and The Gold Medal, and although he had larger successes in Mere Jeevan Saathi and The Train, it is the low-budget spy films — Surakksha, Wardat — that are remembered, their stunts and effects part of the appeal. He directed 24 more films after Farz, finishing with Duty in 1986. His one film in this filmography, Pyar Ki Kahani (1971), belongs to Bachchan's first two years, before he was anyone in particular; nothing in Nagaich's article records the encounter. The infobox repeats his birth date in the death field, so dates come from the lead. Graded High for the biography, Low for the collaboration.

name: Ribhu Dasgupta
career_background: Born in Kolkata, an Indian film and television director. He made his directorial debut with the 2011 film Michael, for which he was nominated at the Shanghai International Film Festival for the Asian New Talent Award for Best Film, and directed the television mini-series Yudh for Sony Entertainment Television in 2013–14.
debut: Michael (2011).
major_works: Michael (2011); Yudh (2013–14, television); Te3n (2016)
recurring_themes: Grief, obsession and investigation; his best-known work turns on a loss that will not resolve.
creative_style: A director who came to features through television, working in muted, rain-soaked Kolkata settings with a slow investigative structure.
major_awards: Nominated for the Asian New Talent Award for Best Film at the Shanghai International Film Festival for Michael.
historical_importance: Modest, though Yudh was an unusual attempt to bring a major film star into a serialised Indian television drama.
relationship_with_actor: One film, but the second collaboration between them. Dasgupta directed Bachchan in the television mini-series Yudh in 2013–14, and then in Te3n (2016), where Bachchan plays John Biswas, an old man who has spent eight years pursuing the unsolved kidnapping and death of his granddaughter, opposite Nawazuddin Siddiqui and Vidya Balan. The film is an official remake of the 2013 South Korean thriller Montage. Television falls outside this workbook's scope, so Yudh appears in no sheet, but it means Te3n was made by a director and actor who already knew each other's working methods.
most_important_collaboration: Te3n (2016), the only one of their two collaborations within this workbook's scope.
biography: Ribhu Dasgupta directs for both film and television, debuting with Michael in 2011 and drawing a Shanghai festival nomination for it. His connection to Bachchan runs through two projects, only one of which this workbook records: he directed him first in Yudh, a Sony television mini-series in 2013–14, and then in Te3n (2016), an adaptation of the South Korean thriller Montage in which Bachchan plays a grandfather who has spent eight years refusing to let an unsolved child abduction rest. It is one of the strongest of his late lead performances, opposite Nawazuddin Siddiqui as a policeman turned priest. Because television is out of scope, the roster counts one film where the working relationship covers two productions. His Wikipedia article is a two-sentence stub that mentions neither, and the substance here comes from a supplementary search. Graded Medium.

name: Rituparno Ghosh
career_background: Born in Calcutta on 31 August 1963 and died there of a heart attack on 30 May 2013. After a degree in economics he began as a creative artist at an advertising agency before turning to film in 1992. He was one of the openly homosexual public figures in Indian cinema. He was influenced by Satyajit Ray, was an avid reader of Rabindranath Tagore — whose work is frequently referenced in his films — and made a documentary, Jeevan Smriti, on Tagore's life.
debut: Directing from 1992; his breakthrough was his second feature, Unishe April, which won the National Film Award for Best Feature Film.
major_works: Unishe April (1994); Dahan (1997); Asukh (1999); Utsab (2000); Shubho Mahurat (2003); Chokher Bali (2003); The Last Lear (2007)
recurring_themes: Domestic interiors and the fault lines inside families, particularly between mothers and daughters and between women of different generations; Tagore adaptations; and, later, gender and sexual identity.
creative_style: An intimate chamber filmmaker working in long conversational scenes and closely observed middle-class Bengali households, in the line of descent from Satyajit Ray.
major_awards: Nineteen National Awards by the article's own count in one sentence and twelve in another, including Best Feature Film for Unishe April (1995), Best Screenplay and Best Bengali Film for Dahan (1998), Best Bengali Film for Asukh (2000), Best Direction for Utsab (2001), Best Bengali Film for Shubho Mahurat (2003) and an award for Chokher Bali (2004).
historical_importance: With Aparna Sen and Goutam Ghose he led the revival of Bengali cinema after Ray, and he was among the very few openly gay figures of stature in the Indian industry.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it is the most unusual on Bachchan's late list. The Last Lear (2007), adapted from Utpal Dutt's play Aajker Shahjahan, casts him as a retired Shakespearean stage actor coaxed into a film role he does not respect, with Preity Zinta and Arjun Rampal in support — an English-language art film in which a screen star plays a theatre actor's contempt for the screen. The article records Bachchan's tribute after Ghosh's death: he remembered him as the only director who had worked with every member of the Bachchan family.
most_important_collaboration: The Last Lear (2007), his only film with Bachchan.
biography: Rituparno Ghosh was the central figure of post-Ray Bengali cinema, winning National Awards from Unishe April onward for a body of work built on domestic interiors, women's lives and Tagore, and he was one of the few openly homosexual public figures in the Indian industry. His single film with Amitabh Bachchan, The Last Lear, is an English-language adaptation of an Utpal Dutt play in which Bachchan plays an old Shakespearean stage actor persuaded into a film he disdains — a piece of casting that sets a screen icon to voicing the theatre's case against the screen. Ghosh died of a heart attack in 2013 at 49, and Bachchan's tribute is preserved in the article: he was the only director who had worked with every member of the Bachchan family. His article contradicts itself on his award count, giving 19 National Awards in one place and 12 in another; both are recorded rather than reconciled. Graded High.

name: Rohit Shetty
career_background: Born in Mangaluru, Karnataka, on 14 March 1974 and working since 1991, a director, screenwriter, stuntman, producer and television personality in Hindi cinema whose films mix action comedy and masala.
debut: Zameen (2003); his breakthrough was Golmaal (2006).
major_works: Golmaal (2006) and its sequels in 2008, 2010 and 2017; Singham (2011); All the Best: Fun Begins (2009); Bol Bachchan (2012); Chennai Express (2013); Singham Returns (2014); Simmba (2018); Sooryavanshi (2021)
recurring_themes: Slapstick ensembles and incorruptible policemen; since Singham he has built a connected 'Cop Universe' across multiple films.
creative_style: A stuntman's cinema of vehicular destruction, broad comedy and unembarrassed spectacle, made repeatedly with Ajay Devgn and at consistently large scale.
major_awards: His awards tables list Best Director nominations for Chennai Express at the Filmfare, Producers Guild, BIG Star and Bollywood Hungama awards, all with blank Result cells, so no win is asserted.
historical_importance: One of the most commercially reliable directors in Hindi cinema; Chennai Express became the highest-grossing Hindi film on release, surpassing 3 Idiots, and the Cop Universe is the industry's most successful shared franchise.
relationship_with_actor: One film, in which Bachchan plays himself. Bol Bachchan (2012) is a comedy of mistaken identity starring Ajay Devgn and Abhishek Bachchan whose title puns on the Bachchan name; Amitabh Bachchan makes a self appearance. The article's several Bachchan mentions refer to Abhishek and to the title rather than to Amitabh, and the film is Abhishek's vehicle, not his father's.
most_important_collaboration: Bol Bachchan (2012), his only film in this filmography.
biography: Rohit Shetty is the most dependable maker of large commercial Hindi films of his generation — the Golmaal comedies, the Singham police films and the Cop Universe they grew into, and Chennai Express, which on release was the highest-grossing Hindi film ever made. A stuntman's son who worked his way up from 1991, he directs action as physical comedy and comedy as controlled chaos. His single point of contact with this filmography is Bol Bachchan, a 2012 farce built around Ajay Devgn and Abhishek Bachchan whose very title plays on the family name, and in which Amitabh Bachchan appears as himself. It is a guest turn in someone else's film, and the article's mentions of 'Bachchan' mostly concern Abhishek. Every result cell in the awards tables is blank, so no win is claimed. Graded High.

name: S. S. Balan
industry: Tamil media and cinema; Hindi cinema
career_background: Born S. Balasubramanian in Madras on 28 December 1935 and died in Chennai on 19 December 2014. He had a six-decade career in Indian media as editor of the Tamil magazine Ananda Vikatan and as managing director of Gemini Studios from the 1950s, later serving as chairman of the Vikatan Group. He was also a political analyst.
debut: Not established as a director; his film work sits alongside a much larger publishing career.
major_works: Sanjog (1972); Sirithu Vazha Vendum (1974)
recurring_themes: Remakes across languages — both of his located films are adaptations of material from another industry.
creative_style: No source characterises his direction; he was a media executive who directed occasionally rather than a career filmmaker.
major_awards: None located.
historical_importance: Substantial, but as a magazine editor and studio head rather than a director: Ananda Vikatan is among the most influential Tamil publications, and Gemini Studios was one of the major studios of south Indian cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film in this filmography and a striking second connection outside it. Sanjog (1972) is a Gemini Studios production he directed, a remake of K. Balachander's Tamil film Iru Kodugal, in which Bachchan plays Mohan, who marries Mala Sinha's Asha in a temple against his mother's wishes and is separated from her; R. D. Burman wrote the music and Aruna Irani co-starred. Two years later Balan directed Sirithu Vazha Vendum (1974), the Tamil remake of Zanjeer, with M. G. Ramachandran in the role that had made Bachchan a star. He therefore directed Bachchan in one film and, in another, directed the Tamil star playing Bachchan's most famous part.
most_important_collaboration: Sanjog (1972), his only film with Bachchan.
biography: S. S. Balan spent sixty years in Indian media as editor of Ananda Vikatan, managing director of Gemini Studios and later chairman of the Vikatan Group, and directed films on the side. His identification in this roster took some care: the short description calls him a journalist and political analyst and the article never mentions Bachchan, but two details confirm it — Sanjog, the 1972 film counted here, was a Gemini Studios production, and the Zanjeer article's remake table credits him with directing Sirithu Vazha Vendum, the 1974 Tamil version of Zanjeer starring M. G. Ramachandran. That gives him an unusual double relationship to this filmography: he directed Bachchan in a temple-marriage melodrama remade from K. Balachander, and then directed the Tamil remake of the film that had made Bachchan a star. A separate coincidence links him to PERSON-298: T. J. Gnanavel, director of Bachchan's Tamil debut fifty-two years later, was a journalist at Ananda Vikatan. Graded High.

name: Sajid Khan
career_background: Born Sajid Kamran Khan in Mumbai on 23 November 1970, a director, television presenter, comedian and actor in the Hindi film industry. He was a judge on the reality show Nach Baliye and a contestant on Bigg Boss 16 in 2022. He is the brother of the choreographer and director Farah Khan.
debut: Heyy Babyy (2007).
major_works: Heyy Babyy (2007); the Housefull series; Humshakals (2014)
recurring_themes: Broad ensemble farce, mistaken identity and slapstick.
creative_style: A comedian-turned-director working in large-cast comedies aimed squarely at a mass audience.
major_awards: None located.
historical_importance: Commercially successful in comedy; his Wikipedia article also carries a section on allegations of sexual harassment, which is noted here without being summarised.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and they share no footage. He directed one of the six stories in Darna Zaroori Hai (2006), the Ram Gopal Varma portmanteau horror with seven credited directors. Bachchan appears only in the frame narrative, as Professor Sunil Khanna, which Varma himself directed. He is also Farah Khan's brother, and she is PERSON-257 in this roster — the two siblings each have exactly one Bachchan credit, and in neither does Bachchan play a conventional role for them.
most_important_collaboration: Darna Zaroori Hai (2006), his only film in this filmography.
biography: Sajid Khan came to directing from television presenting and stand-up comedy, and has worked almost entirely in broad ensemble farce — Heyy Babyy, the Housefull films, Humshakals. His single credit in this filmography is a segment of Darna Zaroori Hai, one of four rows in this roster produced by that one anthology and its seven directors, and like the others it records a shared credit rather than a working relationship: Bachchan's scenes as the storytelling professor belong to the frame narrative Ram Gopal Varma directed. He is the brother of Farah Khan, PERSON-257, which makes them the only siblings in the roster who each directed a Bachchan film — she a self-appearance in Om Shanti Om, he a segment Bachchan is not in. His article carries a section on allegations of sexual harassment, noted here and not detailed. Graded Medium.

name: Sanjay Leela Bhansali
career_background: Born Sanjay Navin Bhansali in Bombay on 24 February 1963, a filmmaker and music composer in Hindi cinema, active since 1996. Leela, in his professional name, is a matronymic. He has received seven National Film Awards and thirteen Filmfare Awards and a BAFTA nomination, and was honoured with the Padma Shri in 2015.
debut: Khamoshi: The Musical (1996).
major_works: Khamoshi: The Musical (1996); Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam (1999); Devdas (2002); Black (2005); Bajirao Mastani (2015); Padmaavat (2018); Gangubai Kathiawadi (2022)
recurring_themes: Doomed grand passion staged at enormous scale; disability and confinement; period spectacle in which colour and set design carry the emotional argument.
creative_style: The most maximalist director in Hindi cinema — vast sets, saturated palettes, operatic performance and music he often composes himself. Period drama is his natural register.
major_awards: Seven National Film Awards and thirteen Filmfare Awards; the Padma Shri (2015); Devdas won the National Film Award for Best Popular Film Providing Wholesome Entertainment and was nominated for the BAFTA Award for Best Film Not in the English Language.
historical_importance: The defining maker of the modern Hindi period epic, and the director whose films dominate the Filmfare Awards more consistently than any of his contemporaries.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it produced one of the two or three greatest performances of Bachchan's career. Black (2005) casts him as Debraj Sahai, the alcoholic and increasingly senile teacher who brings a deaf-blind girl, played by Rani Mukerji, into language and then loses his own mind to Alzheimer's. His article records that Black broke his own Devdas record by taking 11 awards, the highest number ever given to a single film at the Filmfare Awards. The workbook records the film as having no meaningful romance despite its physical intensity, the relationship being a teacher's and a pupil's.
most_important_collaboration: Black (2005), his only film with Bachchan.
biography: Sanjay Leela Bhansali is the great maximalist of contemporary Hindi cinema, with seven National Film Awards, thirteen Filmfare Awards and a Padma Shri, and a body of work — Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam, Devdas, Bajirao Mastani, Padmaavat, Gangubai Kathiawadi — in which enormous sets and saturated colour carry the emotional weight. His single film with Amitabh Bachchan is the exception to all of that: Black, shot in near-monochrome, in which Bachchan plays a violent, drunken, brilliant teacher who drags a deaf-blind child into language and then loses himself to Alzheimer's. It swept the Filmfare Awards with 11 wins, a record for a single film by his article's account, and it is the performance that reopened the second half of Bachchan's career as a character actor. The workbook records Black as having no romance row, the central relationship being teacher and pupil. Graded High.

name: Shankar Mukherjee
career_background: Nothing has been established. No Wikipedia article, no birth or death date, no training and no second credit could be located; a bare Wikipedia fetch returned the error page.
debut: Not established.
major_works: Faraar (1975)
recurring_themes: Not determinable from one film.
creative_style: No source describes his direction.
major_awards: None located.
historical_importance: None established for him personally, though the film he directed travelled: it was remade in Malayalam by Priyadarshan as Parayanumvayya Parayathirikkanumvayya.
relationship_with_actor: One film. Faraar (1975), produced by Alankar Chitra and released on 21 November 1975, casts Bachchan in the lead alongside Sharmila Tagore and Sanjeev Kumar, with music by Kalyanji–Anandji — a crime drama made in the year of Deewaar and Sholay, when he was becoming the biggest star in the country. Nothing records any working relationship beyond the credit.
most_important_collaboration: Faraar (1975), his only film with Bachchan.
biography: Shankar Mukherjee directed Faraar, released in November 1975 with Amitabh Bachchan, Sharmila Tagore and Sanjeev Kumar and music by Kalyanji–Anandji, and beyond that credit the record is empty: no article, no dates, no second film, no biographical detail of any kind. The film itself has had an afterlife he has not — Priyadarshan remade it in Malayalam as Parayanumvayya Parayathirikkanumvayya. Its timing is the most that can be said of the collaboration: 1975 was the year of Deewaar and Sholay, and Faraar is one of the films Bachchan made while becoming the dominant figure in Hindi cinema. The workbook flagged Faraar's Wikipedia plot in phase 2 as reading like an unsourced retelling, so even the film article is used with care. Graded Unknown for the person, Low for the credit.

name: Shashi Kapoor
career_background: Born Balbir Raj Kapoor in Calcutta on 18 March 1938 and died in Mumbai on 4 December 2017. The youngest son of Prithviraj Kapoor, he began as a child actor in 1948 in his brother Raj Kapoor's first film as director, Aag, and had his first adult role in 1961 in Yash Chopra's Dharmputra, establishing himself in 1965 with Waqt and Jab Jab Phool Khile. He is considered one of the greatest actors in the history of Hindi cinema and was also a producer of art cinema.
debut: As director, Ajooba (1991) — his only film as director.
major_works: As actor: Deewaar (1975), Kabhie Kabhie (1976), Kaala Patthar (1979), Suhaag (1979), Namak Halaal (1982). As director and producer: Ajooba (1991)
recurring_themes: As a producer he backed parallel cinema; as a director he attempted large-scale fantasy adventure.
creative_style: Ajooba, his only directorial work, is a costume fantasy made as an Indo-Soviet co-production — an attempt at spectacle far outside the register of the films he produced.
major_awards: Four National Film Awards and two Filmfare Awards; the Padma Bhushan in 2011 and the Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 2014.
historical_importance: A major actor of Hindi cinema and a significant patron of its art-cinema wing, honoured with the industry's highest award.
relationship_with_actor: One credit in this roster and roughly a dozen films together outside it. The article records that from 1975 Kapoor formed a hit pair with Bachchan, the two making Deewaar, Kabhie Kabhie, Immaan Dharam, Kaala Patthar, Suhaag and Namak Halaal among others — a partnership that defined a decade of Hindi cinema. The roster counts only Ajooba (1991), which Kapoor directed and produced and in which Bachchan plays the masked Shehzada Ali, because acting is not a collaborator function this workbook tracks. The article records that Kapoor asked Bachchan to star in his directorial debut and that Bachchan, who was not signing new films at the time, made an exception because of their friendship. The film was an expensive failure.
most_important_collaboration: Ajooba (1991), his only film as Bachchan's director, made on the strength of a fifteen-year friendship.
biography: Shashi Kapoor was one of the finest actors of his generation, the youngest son of Prithviraj Kapoor, a Padma Bhushan and Dadasaheb Phalke laureate, and the producer who financed a significant part of Indian parallel cinema. He also made exactly one film as director: Ajooba, an Indo-Soviet fantasy adventure co-directed with the Russian Gennady Vasilyev (PERSON-258), which he produced and which failed badly. That is the credit this roster counts, and the article supplies the reason it exists — Kapoor asked Bachchan to star, and Bachchan agreed out of friendship despite having stopped signing films.
